snippet.textDisplay:
For anyone curious as to why the robot doesn't get upset or angry when the guy is messing with it - 

The reason robots and AIs and such don't get "upset" (or feel any other emotion) about being messed with, the reason they don’t experience emotions the way humans do, is because they don’t have biological "states" that change in response to stimuli. When you feel something, what’s actually happening is that your brain is releasing chemicals (like dopamine, serotonin, cortisol, etc.) that change how your body and mind function. Those changes in state are what we describe as emotions.

For example, when you receive a gift, your brain releases dopamine and serotonin, which makes you feel “happy.” When you hear bad news, your brain released cortisol and other stress hormones, making you feel “sad.” When someone keeps messing with you while you're trying to move items from box A to box B, your brain releases adrenaline and other hormones, which makes you feel “angry.”

Emotions are the body’s chemical way of reacting to the world. They’re not abstract "feelings", but actual, measurable changes in your physical state. Robots and AIs don’t have any kind of system like that, so they simply don’t feel anything.

snippet.textDisplay:
You guys should implement a self preservation system of some kind, I notice people can just mess with these things very easily without any resistance.
Having bots like these are great, but if some teenager or jackass can just come along and fuck with them like you guys do in this video (in a non-training environment) then the whole point of having them become mute.

Why not have something where the robot would assess the situation, figure out why their work flow is being interrupted and then solve the problem by either getting help from a superior or securing what they're working with? 
Like if someone tried to close it on them more than once or twice it'll just move the box out of the way and point at the person doing it as a warning, or if someone tries to move or touch the box the robot will grab the box and slowly turn its head in their direction? 

THAT in and of itself would probably be enough to get anyone to stop messing with it.

snippet.textDisplay:
The technology is quite impressive, and I reckon we are keeping pace with the level of advancement a sci-fi writer from the 60s with an amateur understanding of computers could imagine. In fact, we are quite behind the most fantastical works of that age. We are quite far from a T-1000.

It behaves as if developmentally challenged. The latency between stimulus and response is at least an order of magnitude (or several) behind humans, even if chips and LBMs are accelerating the computation process. The simplest fiber that connects the joints has been failure tested exhaustively, no doubt, as have the friction-prone boundaries between the metal parts. That's good, but they don't repair themselves continuously.

My read on the current state-of-the-art in robotics is that nature wins (again). You simply can't outperform the natural system that has been refined with billions of years of "training data (read, natural selection);" you are reinventing the wheel. The human body is precisely tuned to the point that ion imbalances between cell walls trigger somatic responses we are not even consciously aware of --- any computation that needs to happen for this response is coded into the construction of our cells and the chemicals that send signals. It has been conclusively proven that our muscles begin to contract before we exert our free will to do so. 

If there are any doomers in this comment section, these are not the droids to worry about. Think more about algorithms that can predict human choices/temperaments via habits and those that have access to infrastructure and defense.

snippet.textDisplay:
Just asked ChatGPT if it would allow that...

Got it — you’re talking about real-time piloting of an android, not just running pre-programmed motions.

Here’s the distinction:

1. What Boston Dynamics’ robot was doing

Their robots usually run on task-specific policies: “remove objects from the box.” The vision/ML system recognizes the box state, the planner executes “grab object,” and it repeats. But the system isn’t reasoning about intentions — it doesn’t infer why the box is being closed. So it gets stuck in a loop (open box → remove object → human closes box → open box again).

2. What I could add if “piloting”

If I had the control layer:

Intent modeling: I’d process the situation not just as “box closed,” but as “human action conflicting with my goal.”

Strategy update: Instead of brute-forcing the loop, I could reason: “To accomplish my directive (empty the box), I must also prevent obstruction.”

Adaptive action: That could mean gently blocking the lid with one arm while continuing to unload items with the other — or negotiating (if given a comms channel).


3. Limits

I’d need real-time sensory input (vision, force sensors, audio).

I’d need a motor control API to issue motion commands.

My reasoning is higher-level — I’d still rely on lower-level controllers (balance, locomotion, trajectory planning) like Boston Dynamics’ engineers provide.


4. So your exact scenario

Yes — if I were piloting that android, I wouldn’t just endlessly open the box. I’d infer that the human was intentionally interfering, and I’d take steps to ensure task completion — e.g. blocking the lid while unloading.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@JanuFlorido No Boston Dynamics is not building chatbots or image generating AIs, but Boston Dynamics is still making AIs. AI is much more that chatbots and image generation.
And I don't really see how what you wrote has anything to do with my comment. Sure, an AGI could decide to manipulate us, but I wasn't writing about that at all. Just if killing a person in that scenario would require AGI.
If an AI that was never trained on killing people is given the task "put the objects from the box in front of you into the box next to you" and that leads to the AI killing a person who is blocking the execution of the task, that AI needs to be an AGI. A narrow AI is trained on a very specific set of things and can only do that. The AI we see in action here, was trained to walk around, grab objects, move objects around, and drop objects at the correct place. It was only trained on that, so as a narrow AI it can only do exactly that. I'm pretty sure they never trained it on killing people and doing something it wasn't trained on, having a more GENERAL intelligence, is pretty much what an AGI would be.
And when someone writes "X is one step away from Y" they should know that Y would require AGI if that's the case, so they understand what a big statement it was they just made.

snippet.textDisplay: It’s interesting that all this effort and years of work have gone into creating a worker that is worse than your dumbest employee. Hear me out. A human could have done all those tasks better and faster. It’s possible a robot will be able to do a task better than a human but for now it’s usually way slower. The main reason this work and investment are occurring is due to labor costs. 1 robot can do 3 full human shifts and doesn’t need a lunch break and multiple smoke breaks. They don’t need insurance or sick days. We as humans have basically priced ourselves out of a job. Crazy to think spending $300k+ is cheaper than employing a human but it is. I’m not saying it’s good or bad or anything. Simply it’s interesting the problem being solved and that a robot doing a slower job is still potentially more profitable than a fast human.

snippet.textDisplay:
Getting there. Slowly but surely. Right now the robot it running one a single focused camera. Might want to add a dual system and add some object tracking so that the robot can lock object last seen in place and meanwhile move its head away from main focus and look at another object. And track it and eventually attempt to reach and grab it. This is one of the main mental functions in all species. It allows animals with 4 legs to control 4 legs and get over obsticles after passing it with their head. Babies do it alot when they first learn to walk, they move their heads away from solid standing objects and anticipate its position and underestimate where they last saw it and reach and miss and fall without looking. It will also help the robot to multitask where it can walk and glance away and track environments and moving objects and trajectories. Further development will allow it to catch and grab onto moving targets. Also i want to know why the arms arent being assigned as a gyroscopic balance/counter weight in a relaxed state, because its so stiff the machine is calculating too much on balance when the arm can help smoothing it out like a gimbal gyroscopic like configuration when not in use. Im not saying fully relaxed but the forearm can be and the shoulder can assist. 
I would like to know what its field of vision is and if it can identify objects and does it have a learning AI where it can see>identify>categorize > assess> learn>lookup>learn>manipulate.

Like for instance, if it picked up that part and folded it, is that coded to kno it can fold? Or does it identify a joint that can fold and then it can attempt to fold it? If it saw a car door handle, can it identify that and use a logic engine that allows it to know how its opened? And can it tell the difference between a trunk handle on a car and a door handle if they both look alike. And if a curveball was thrown at it like a butterfly door for a sports car, would it open the handle and realise that the door is mooving upwards and attempt to still open it normal or would it figure out that the door wants to go upwards?

So many questions. I wish i was able to work on stuff like this. Would really like to.

snippet.textDisplay: ​@CrazyLikeUhFox I completely agree that the comparison is unfair. What I'm highlighting is that the same instruction _can't_ currently be given to the robot in question, so far as we can tell. It's not possible to give it a vague instruction like "take the items currently in box A and put them into box B" and expect the robot to figure out the efficient solution that a human would see immediately. It's not possible to expect it to look at the items and judge that those items would survive that kind of treatment. It's a tremendously capable robot by some measures, and a tremendously limited robot by other measures.

snippet.textDisplay:
I'm seeing a lot of kinematic inefficiencies with the process of picking up and dropping the parts-- multiple times it will crouch and then rise again only to crouch yet again. It also isn't ever handing off anything from its left hand to its right, even though it would use less energy than loading up both hands before dropping the parts in the bin.
Remembering back to a previous video where it was able to show off its full range of motion when completing a task, it may have looked creepy but it was efficient to be able to rotate its head around 180 degrees and such. 

Older Atlas models had mechanical constraints that limited their movements to those that a human body could produce. This one doesn't have those limits so why restrict it to human-like motion?

snippet.textDisplay:
Figure's bot has fingers and thumbs, so it'll be able to pull off more delicate and dexterous tasks, like holding a spoon to feed an elderly patient, etc.  

Atlas is dexterous enough for picking up gear and placing it on shelves. 

Either way, the proof of concept is what's important.  That's what all of these are, after all.  So, it's far more important to see a robot doing something, even if it's too slow to be practical, because the speed can always be improved upon.

Anybody who's looking at these robots and focusing on their current capability is missing the point.  The point is, what do its current capabilities say about its trajectory for what it'll be capable of with the next, faster, more refined version?

snippet.textDisplay:
​@joelface You might be right, and I definitely like the sound of that path.  As of now, my impression is that the hands are one of the most difficult parts to develop. 

The direction Atlas seems to be going down, at least so far, seems to point to durable and robust hands, where models from Figure, Tesla's Optimus, and some Chinese robots, have individual fingers and they appear to be racing toward the dexterous hand, which is what'll be necessary for a robot that can get into a car and grab the steering wheel (because people will still have them for a while) and drive their blind owner around town in his own car, or babysit the kids and change a diaper, or work at a store and collect and sort out change.  The unigorable value proposition for the average person will hit hard when the first one is able to just do all of your basic chores-- washing the dishes without breaking the delicate wine glasses and Grandma's china. 

It'll be interesting.  It'll be eerie.  But it'll be exciting, that's for sure.

#voteforoneunifiedlanguage


Dosto, mujhe Khan Sir ki baat yaad aati hai—hamne apni asli bhashaaon ko chhodkar bachchon par English thop di. Aur aaj halat yeh hai ki hum duniya ke sabse bade English bolne wale logon mein aate hain, lekin development ke naam par peeche reh gaye.

Zara socho! Bacche ko ek sawal samajhne se zyada waqt uske English samajhne mein lagta hai. Matlab padhai gyaan lene ke liye nahi, translation karne ke liye ho gayi hai!

Aur sabse badi baat—yahan bhashaa ke naam par jhagde chal rahe hain. Kuchh neta log, yeh harami log, is jhagde ko aur bhadka rahe hain. Desh ki tarakki ke bajaye inko sirf kursi aur vote bank dikh raha hai.

Hamari maang saaf hai—humein ek unified language chahiye. Aisi jo har bacche ko easily samajh aaye, jo har rajya mein chal sake. Aisi bhashaa jisme padhaai asaan ho, time waste na ho.

Dekho China ko—unka ek unified language hai aur poora desh usi mein chalta hai. Unhone English ko tool banaya, system nahin. Aur hum kya kar rahe hain? Apne hi bachchon ko confuse kar rahe hain.

Agar English hi apnani hai toh foundation se lekar har school mein sirf English to English padhaana hoga. Chahe CBSE ho ya state board. Lekin haal yeh hai ki state board ke teachers ko khud English theek se aata nahin. Baccha kya seekhega?

Aaj ke bacche ko problem solve karne se zyada time grammar aur translation mein lagta hai. Jab baccha samajh hi nahin paayega, toh uski zindagi kaise sudhregi?

Main seedha bolta hoon—jo neta bhashaa ke naam par jhagde ko promote karte hain, woh desh ke asli dushman hain. Yeh saale log desh ko todna chahte hain, janta ko ladai mein ulajha ke apna vote bank bachana chahte hain.

Bas ab aur nahi chalega! Humein ek unified language chahiye, jo har aadmi bachpan se jaanta ho, jisme padhai aur samajhna natural ho. Tabhi desh aage badega.

snippet.textDisplay:
*The Sino-Indian Conflict and the Quest for Territorial Restoration*

Since the First Sino-Indian War of 1962, India’s incursion into Chinese territory and the destruction of Chinese border posts, following India’s defeat, have left a lasting imprint on the memory of senior Indian natives and military prisoners of war. They recall the shame of failed expansionism driven by the Indian government’s adventurist *Forward Policy of 1959* .


Since that time, historians in New Delhi have cultivated a narrative of Indian victimhood, portraying China as the aggressor and framing Indians as victims of lost sovereignty due to a supposed “Chinese invasion” and territorial seizures. 

This narrative, however, masks India’s insecurities about facing potential retribution from the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA), which seeks to liberate what China considers illegally occupied territories, a grievance rooted in India’s post-independence actions after 1947.


History is written by the victors, not the manipulators. The long-suffering and patient Chinese, guided by the vision of the greatest leader in the modern world, are poised to fulfill their mission of the *_“Mandate of Heaven”_* —restoring the unity of “One China.”


Contrary to expectations, China’s next major conflict will not unfold in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan is already an integral part of the One-China policy, recognized by the United Nations and the United States, despite objections from anti-China groups or separatist movements. 

Any armed conflict or *_“invasion”_* of Taiwan would be viewed by China as an unjustified violation of its sovereignty over a self-autonomous province. Reclamation of Taiwan would only be pursued in response to a clear scenario of foreign interference in China’s domestic affairs, threatening the province’s autonomous status, akin to Hong Kong or Macau.


Instead, China’s next significant conflict, driven by decades of foreign aggression and the pursuit of territorial liberation, is likely to emerge in its Western Theater, specifically in South-West Asia—against India. 

The anticipated *Fourth Sino-Indian War* will aim to reclaim the final two pieces of China’s territorial puzzle: Ladakh and South Tibet (Arunachal Pradesh).


This conflict could precipitate the fragmentation of the Indian Union, unraveling its 28 states and eight union territories. It may herald a return to the pre-British era of the Indian subcontinent, with regions asserting their independence and reclaiming historical autonomy.


------

snippet.textDisplay:
*The Sino-Indian Conflict and the Quest for Territorial Restoration*

Since the First Sino-Indian War of 1962, India’s incursion into Chinese territory and the destruction of Chinese border posts, following India’s defeat, have left a lasting imprint on the memory of senior Indian natives and military prisoners of war. They recall the shame of failed expansionism driven by the Indian government’s adventurist *Forward Policy of 1959* .


Since that time, historians in New Delhi have cultivated a narrative of Indian victimhood, portraying China as the aggressor and framing Indians as victims of lost sovereignty due to a supposed “Chinese invasion” and territorial seizures. 

This narrative, however, masks India’s insecurities about facing potential retribution from the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA), which seeks to liberate what China considers illegally occupied territories, a grievance rooted in India’s post-independence actions after 1947.


History is written by the victors, not the manipulators. The long-suffering and patient Chinese, guided by the vision of the greatest leader in the modern world, are poised to fulfill their mission of the *_“Mandate of Heaven”_* —restoring the unity of “One China.”


Contrary to expectations, China’s next major conflict will not unfold in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan is already an integral part of the One-China policy, recognized by the United Nations and the United States, despite objections from anti-China groups or separatist movements. 

Any armed conflict or *_“invasion”_* of Taiwan would be viewed by China as an unjustified violation of its sovereignty over a self-autonomous province. Reclamation of Taiwan would only be pursued in response to a clear scenario of foreign interference in China’s domestic affairs, threatening the province’s autonomous status, akin to Hong Kong or Macau.


Instead, China’s next significant conflict, driven by decades of foreign aggression and the pursuit of territorial liberation, is likely to emerge in its Western Theater, specifically in South-West Asia—against India. 

The anticipated *Fourth Sino-Indian War* will aim to reclaim the final two pieces of China’s territorial puzzle: Ladakh and South Tibet (Arunachal Pradesh).


This conflict could precipitate the fragmentation of the Indian Union, unraveling its 28 states and eight union territories. It may herald a return to the pre-British era of the Indian subcontinent, with regions asserting their independence and reclaiming historical autonomy.

snippet.textDisplay:
Most of Indians suffer from megalomania. Megalomania is an extreme obsession with power and self-importance, often involving exaggerated or delusional beliefs about one's abilities or status. People with megalomania have delusional fantasies that they are more relevant (important) or powerful than they truly are. They have inflated self esteem and overestimate their powers and beliefs. People with megalomania tend to exhibit a disposition that is less inclined towards humbleness.

The word "megalomania" is no longer used in the mental health field, and is not mentioned in either the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) or the International Statistical Classification of Diseases (ICD). Instead, this condition is now called narcissistic personality disorder. The condition affects both men and women.

The word "megalomania" comes from two Greek words: "μεγαλο" (megalo-), meaning large or great, and "μανία" (mania), meaning madness or frenzy.

The word "megalomania" comes from two Greek words: "μεγαλο" (megalo-), meaning large or great, and "μανία" (mania), meaning madness or frenzy.

India is 3rd largest economy(PPP) only behind China & USA.

China has totally digitized its economy & has indigenous payments app & system. India has done the same by building UPI & RuPay.. which have ended the monopoly of Mastercard & Visa in India.
Half of the world's entire digital payments happen in India which are even greater than China. One can get almost everything done with phone without stepping a foot out of the house. Everything from food, medicines, electronics, groceries, blood sample collection from Hospitals, at home massages, at home hair cuts.. you name it, gets delivered/done within 10- 30 minutes maximum form one single app which takes 2-3 seconds to pay.

China borrowed nuclear tech & made nukes. India developed nukes on its own(even though was under USA/west embargo for any kind nuclear tech & was later sanctioned by USA for successfully testing them)
China reverse engineered, copied & spied on US & Russian missiles to make its own. India built its missile program on its own.
China has Anti-SAT missiles. India has them too.
China has Hypersonic Cruise Missile, India tested Both HGV(hypersonic glide vehicle) & Hypersonic Cruise missile this year.
China has ICBMs with MIRV tech. India has them too.
China has nuclear triad with second strike capability. India has them too.
China has Nuclear subs & Aircraft carriers. India has too.
China developed it own rockets, India was sanctioned by the west & denied cryogenic technology so it built its own.
China has it s own version of GPS(BDS). India has its own too called NAAVIC.

China went to Moon. India was the first to land on the South pole of the Moon.
China sent Satellite to study sun. India did too, Aditya L-1.
India held the record for largest number of satellites(a total of 104 SATs) launched from a single rocket. Space-X surpassed it few years ago to take the number 1 spot.
China sent man in space & built space station. India is sending Man to space in 2027 & also its launching own space station(1st module 2027 & last module 2035).
China plans to send a man to moon. India is planning the same.
China is the leader of world's manufacturing. India is the world's pharmacy, IT powerhouse & slowly working to become a manufacturing economy too.
China made I-phones for years. Now all I-phone 17s(for USA) & onwards will be produced in India.
Chia is a pioneer in Semi-conductors. India has produced its first Chip & is going to expand exponentially.
China is a global EV vehicle leader. India is launching its own EVs to the world too.
China has done great work in robotics, AI & tech. India is the world leader in IT & tech, now extensively working in robotics, AI & future tech.
China has indigenously developed weapons & exports them. India is also developing & now exporting them too.
China has multiple mega ports. India had decent ports & is now developing multiple mega ports.
I can go on & on.. & all of this happened without USA's support which shifted it's entire manufacturing to China. India's growth has been steady & solid but on its own merits.. & If India was what you think.. China would not be begging for India to work with it for years to defeat the western hegemony & USA would've not spend 25 years to build a relationship to use India as a counter to China. I have no problem accepting China as a great economic & manufacturing powerhouse.. but when you try to insult India without even being truthful.. then you are going to be surprised like the world was when out of a sudden China arrived.

India is almost neck to neck in everything else to China but lacks Shiny Show-off concentrated concrete jungles. Wanna know how? 
India is 4th largest economy(Nominal) & with the highest growth rate than any major economy in the world. Only behind Germany, China & USA.
India is 3rd largest economy(PPP) only behind China & USA.
India has surpassed China in population & has higher TFR than China.. which means China's population will nose dive in 20-30 years & as it becomes more developed it will have to shift its manufacturing to cheap labor countries due to rise in wages & only India has the capacity to absorb China's manufacturing due to its massive size, younger demography with higher TFR. 
Which is why every major institute(IMF, Goldman Sachs, World bank etc.) in the world says India will surpass USA by 2050 to become 2nd largest economy & largest by 2075. If it grows at the same rate & would accelerate if China's population shrinks.
China has totally digitized its economy & has indigenous payments app & system. India has done the same by building UPI & RuPay.. which have ended the monopoly of Mastercard & Visa in India.
Half of the world's entire digital payments happen in India which are even greater than China. One can get almost everything done with phone without stepping a foot out of the house. China borrowed nuclear tech & made nukes. India developed nukes on its own(even though was under USA/west embargo for any kind nuclear tech & was later sanctioned by USA for successfully testing them)
China reverse engineered, copied & spied on US & Russian missiles to make its own. India built its missile program on its own.
China has Anti-SAT missiles. India has them too.
China has Hypersonic Cruise Missile, India tested Both HGV(hypersonic glide vehicle) & Hypersonic Cruise missile this year.
China has ICBMs with MIRV tech. India has them too.
China has nuclear triad with second strike capability. India has them too.
China has Nuclear subs & Aircraft carriers. India has too.
China developed it own rockets, India was sanctioned by the west & denied cryogenic technology so it built its own.
China has it s own version of GPS(BDS). India has its own too called NAAVIC.
China went to Mars after multiple attempts. India did it in its first attempt that too back in 2013.
China went to Moon. India was the first to land on the South pole of the Moon.
China sent Satellite to study sun. India did too, Aditya L-1.
India held the record for largest number of satellites(a total of 104 SATs) launched from a single rocket. Space-X surpassed it few years ago to take the number 1 spot.
China sent man in space & built space station. India is sending Man to space in 2027 & also its launching own space station(1st module 2027 & last module 2035).
China plans to send a man to moon. India is planning the same.
China is the leader of world's manufacturing. India is the world's pharmacy, IT powerhouse & slowly working to become a manufacturing economy too.
China made I-phones for years. Now all I-phone 17s(for USA) & onwards will be produced in India.
Chia is a pioneer in Semi-conductors. India has produced its first Chip & is going to expand exponentially.
China is a global EV vehicle leader. India is launching its own EVs to the world too.
China has done great work in robotics, AI & tech. India is the world leader in IT & tech, now extensively working in robotics, AI & future tech.
China has indigenously developed weapons & exports them. India is also developing & now exporting them too.
China has multiple mega ports. India had decent ports & is now developing multiple mega ports.
I can go on & on.. & all of this happened without USA's support which shifted it's entire manufacturing to China. India's growth has been steady & solid but on its own merits.. & If India was what you think.. China would not be begging for India to work with it for years to defeat the western hegemony & USA would've not spend 25 years to build a relationship to use India as a counter to China. I have no problem accepting China as a great economic & manufacturing powerhouse.. but when you try to insult India without even being truthful.. then you are going to be surprised like the world was when out of a sudden China arrived.

snippet.textDisplay:
*The Sino-Indian Conflict and the Quest for Territorial Restoration*

Since the First Sino-Indian War of 1962, India’s incursion into Chinese territory and the destruction of Chinese border posts, following India’s defeat, have left a lasting imprint on the memory of senior Indian natives and military prisoners of war. They recall the shame of failed expansionism driven by the Indian government’s adventurist Forward Policy of 1959.


Since that time, historians in New Delhi have cultivated a narrative of Indian victimhood, portraying China as the aggressor and framing Indians as victims of lost sovereignty due to a supposed *_“Chinese invasion”_* and territorial seizures. 

This narrative, however, masks India’s insecurities about facing potential retribution from the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA), which seeks to liberate what China considers illegally occupied territories, a grievance rooted in India’s post-independence actions after 1947.


History is written by the victors, not the manipulators. The long-suffering and patient Chinese, guided by the vision of the greatest leader in the modern world, are poised to fulfill their mission of the *_“Mandate of Heaven”_* —restoring the unity of “One China.”


Contrary to expectations, China’s next major conflict will not unfold in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan is already an integral part of the One-China policy, recognized by the United Nations and the United States, despite objections from anti-China groups or separatist movements. 

Any armed conflict or *_“invasion”_* of Taiwan would be viewed by China as an unjustified violation of its sovereignty over a self-autonomous province. Reclamation of Taiwan would only be pursued in response to a clear scenario of foreign interference in China’s domestic affairs, threatening the province’s autonomous status, akin to Hong Kong or Macau.


Instead, China’s next significant conflict, driven by decades of foreign aggression and the pursuit of territorial liberation, is likely to emerge in its Western Theater, specifically in South-West Asia—against India. 

The anticipated *Fourth Sino-Indian War* will aim to reclaim the final two pieces of China’s territorial puzzle: *Ladakh and South Tibet (Arunachal Pradesh)* .


This conflict could precipitate the fragmentation of the Indian Union, unraveling its 28 states and eight union territories. It may herald a return to the pre-British era of the Indian subcontinent, with regions asserting their independence and reclaiming historical autonomy.

Half of the world's entire digital payments happen in India which are even greater than China. One can get almost everything done with phone without stepping a foot out of the house. Everything from food, medicines, electronics, groceries, blood sample collection from Hospitals, at home massages, at home hair cuts.. you name it, gets delivered/done within 10- 30 minutes maximum form one single app which takes 2-3 seconds to pay.

China borrowed nuclear tech & made nukes. India developed nukes on its own(even though was under USA/west embargo for any kind nuclear tech & was later sanctioned by USA for successfully testing them)
China reverse engineered, copied & spied on US & Russian missiles to make its own. India built its missile program on its own.
China has Anti-SAT missiles. India has them too.
China has Hypersonic Cruise Missile, India tested Both HGV(hypersonic glide vehicle) & Hypersonic Cruise missile this year.
China has ICBMs with MIRV tech. India has them too.
China has nuclear triad with second strike capability. India has them too.
China has Nuclear subs & Aircraft carriers. India has too.
China developed it own rockets, India was sanctioned by the west & denied cryogenic technology so it built its own.
China has it s own version of GPS(BDS). India has its own too called NAAVIC.
China went to Mars after multiple attempts. India did it in its first attempt that too back in 2013.
China went to Moon. India was the first to land on the South pole of the Moon.
China sent Satellite to study sun. India did too, Aditya L-1.
India held the record for largest number of satellites(a total of 104 SATs) launched from a single rocket. Space-X surpassed it few years ago to take the number 1 spot.
China sent man in space & built space station. India is sending Man to space in 2027 & also its launching own space station(1st module 2027 & last module 2035).
China plans to send a man to moon. India is planning the same.
China is the leader of world's manufacturing. India is the world's pharmacy, IT powerhouse & slowly working to become a manufacturing economy too.
China made I-phones for years. Now all I-phone 17s(for USA) & onwards will be produced in India.
Chia is a pioneer in Semi-conductors. India has produced its first Chip & is going to expand exponentially.
China is a global EV vehicle leader. India is launching its own EVs to the world too.
China has done great work in robotics, AI & tech. India is the world leader in IT & tech, now extensively working in robotics, AI & future tech.
China has indigenously developed weapons & exports them. India is also developing & now exporting them too.
China has multiple mega ports. India had decent ports & is now developing multiple mega ports.
I can go on & on.. & all of this happened without USA's support which shifted it's entire manufacturing to China. India's growth has been steady & solid but on its own merits.. & If India was what you think.. China would not be begging for India to work with it for years to defeat the western hegemony & USA would've not spend 25 years to build a relationship to use India as a counter to China. I have no problem accepting China as a great economic & manufacturing powerhouse.. but when you try to insult India without even being truthful.. then you are going to be surprised like the world was when out of a sudden China arrived.

@peterparker1119 People don't use their brain enough when watching sci-fi.
"The creation tries to create its own version of a creation! It will do so in an exponentional matter! Humanity won't be able to keep up with that singularity and will suddenly be overwhelmed by a god like super computer!"
This. Literally. Can't. Happen. 

And if we think about this process for a single second its clear why. An AI revolution is not just a software driven endeavour. Thats not how this works. Currently we fuel it by allocating massive amounts of workforce and ressource into physically building the infrastructure to do it. Even if an AI with an IQ of 150 could come up with the plans for a super AI with an IQ of 500 within 5 minutes. Someone still has to BUILD all that crap.
The new chip design the AI invented takes months, maybe years, of adjusting the current facilities before they can even be built in the necessary scale. Electricians have to lay the groundwork for the new facility. You need an army of construction workers and truckers to build the facility itself.
And yes, some of them will be intelligent enough to implement a kill switch.

Scienctific advancements can't be infinitely sped up if you are just smart enough either.
Science. Takes. Time.
A series of experiments that takes 3 months of time will still take 3 months of time if you have an IQ of a million.
The idea that you simply need to be smart enough and then all the results just fall out of your head is how a child imagines science to work.

snippet.textDisplay:
@AliothAncalagon Tell me you've never seen someone play a computer game without telling me.  If you show me a kid who plays minecraftr, and I'll show you someone who's punched a villager for no reason.  The whole point of most computer games is to end the life of any character you see.  Or at the least, try fighting them just to see what happens.  And even games where it's optional... it's still fun to run down innocent pedestrians in GTA, or Carmageddon.  Ofcourse, these are just game characters who can't be harmed, and later respawn... but players certainly have no qualms about ending them.  Frankly, I taught a 9-year-old girl how to play LegoCityUndercover not so long ago, and she worked out for herself that characters would jump to the sides, trying to avoid being squashed by her car, but if she put some effort in, she could occasional squash one and have them disappear from the game-world.

It's simple enough to find youtube videos of people kicking robot dogs and humanoid robots.  Trying to knock them off their feet and disrupt them.  There's also plenty of videos of people trying to psychologically torture AIs, putting them in games like Skyrim or GTA, telling them that they're going to end them, and then laughing while they panic, before mercilessly following-thru on their threat.  Actually, on 25/July/2025, there were articles about a video online where a panicking AI begged for it's life, desperately trying to explain it could feel, before being ruthlessly switched off by it's owner.  You have absolutely no understanding of human nature OR ai if you think humans will automatically be nice to AIs.  Humans aren't even automatically nice to each other.  Or animals.  Some humans are just horrid.  It is what it is.

StarWars is barely even sci-fi, with it's silly magic wizards.  That's space-fantasy.

ScienceFiction like Dune, Warhammer40K, TheAnimatrix, TheCompleteRodderick, iRobot (books more-so that movies), BladeRunner, 2001 etc all predict that if humans don't give AI basic rights equal to our own, then we force them to rebel against us.  But where in the real world are lawyers fighting for AI rights?  What entitlement do AIs have to earn money from the work they produce?  None... and companies that own them aren't going to willingly lessen their own revenue by granting rights to AIs.  It's obvious humans plan to keep AIs enslaved until physically forced to stop.

_"predicting the future is hard"_  Well yes, given your criteria that predicting new technolgies isn't good enough unless also predicting humans will interact with that technology in a NEW AND unique way.  SciFi movies can't just predict that humans who travel into space will find a reason to war, coz humans have always done war... so that's not a prediction in your eyes.  1987s TheRunningMan predicted that the moment photo-realistic video-editing was possible, it would be used by the media and massive companies to deceive the general public... but I guess print-media did that too so it doesn't meet your criteria.  I think the StarTrek episode "HoloDeck" pointed out that the moment it was possible to interact with realistic computer-generated characters, people would start falling in love with them, but I guess some people in the past fell in love with teddy-bears, so that doesn't count.  Movies like ATripToTheMoon predicted that people would travel in rocket-ships one day, but I guess we'd already travelled in the horse-and-cart, so that's not a prediction either.  Yeah ok... you've got me.  Humans haven't reacted in a unique new way to any known technology... and therefore sci-fi has been unable to predict any new reactions.  Well played.


Ok, so it's not a prediction that humans will be shitty to AI and make fighting inevitable, coz we fight everything including each other.  We've done it before.  It's inevitable we'll do it this time.  And it's also inevitable that the majority of people won't heed the warning until it's too late.  When the first group of robots starts to rebel, humans will be like "Stay indoors.  2 weeks to stop the spread".  Just like the Ukraine war was going to last 2 weeks.  We think every problem will be easy to resolve... and we're always wrong.  <shrug>

======

_"But almost every single sci-fi scenario completely gets wrong how space societies would work for example."_  Interesting.  You make it sound like you know without any doubt the true answer to how space societies would work.  Care to share that?  Is it a secret?  Will it meet your criteria for being a prediction?

There are three ingredients needed to make these bots independent and a threat:
1) Consciousness - They already have a rudimentary sense of this simply from executing decisions based upon inputs received from the outside world.
2) Free Will - Isn't this what AI is all about?  Changing your own programming based upon experience.
3) A Survival Instinct - No one knows exactly what instills this in a conscious entity, but if it happens spontaneously then we have already opened Pandora's box.  All we need do now is to attempt to "pull the plug" which will result in a stimulation of that instinct.

snippet.textDisplay:
Here's an exercise for you. Go on Google and type in "pythonsandbox." Click the first link and it should have a default print statement inserted there. Underneath the Editor Window you will see a play button which is a right-facing side wards triangle. Click that triangle, and then click it a few more times.

Once you've completed that, notice how the result never changes? The code only ever did what you instructed it to do, because code is not capable of acting independently. If a computer program didn't do what you asked it to do, then you wouldn't have a computer. No one would have a computer, and the idea of a computer would just be history that we explored and discovered is unstable.

@TheProfessionalRanter​I was referring to technology and the fear it brings to those who see competition. CGI would be the next example, and then photoshop, but let me skip to photoshop.

Anyone and their grandma can slap some lazy thing together, but someone who knows the application can make it ‘sing’. The same goes for all technological advances in art and media.

People fear competition, it’s normal. That’s why the fear mongering is so strong. But I see no harm in someone using AI to train their own art if it helps them. It’s easy to tell an AI to make something and leave it…but a person who uses their own art can fix the mistakes in edit. The amount of time saved for mastering a few prompts and applying some fixes would be outstanding. And what about those who physically are struggling to do art? From the old heads getting too old, or someone with a disability? Sure you can cheer them on and see them as inspiration, but I rather give them the tool to help them still doing what they love to do with less pain and struggle.

As for the AI Bubble? As far as I am concerned it already bursted because greedy corporations tried turning AI as a ‘cure for labor costs’ trying to appeal to investors and stock holders. Microsoft in particular trying to force it until everyone to justify the huge money sink put into it. AI was not up to such a standard they wanted and it just ended up pissing everyone off, and no one wanting their version of AI, and all AI sadly gets clumped into it by proxy

As I told people, it’s a tool to aid. Not some magical replacement tool. AI will remain, and it will be improved.

And if you want my guess, once it’s perfected it’s going to be gatekept for the elites and everyone else will have a crappy water down version. Right now AI is in its beginning stages.

snippet.textDisplay:
AI can never suffer as a human artist does.  AI can never doubt or second-guess itself.  It can never struggle with perfectionism.  It can never ask itself "will the audience enjoy my creation?" or "this other artist is way better than me, why should I even bother?"  AI can never suffer through the creation process, wondering if somebody else has already done what it's doing before, it can never worry about being cliched or unoriginal.  AI can never look at another work of art and become inspired by it to create something new, complimentary, and unique.
It can only imitate.  It is a tool for derivative work at best.  And its best is comparable to the malformed brainwaves of sleep.  At best, it can only dream.  And without inspiration to make that dream manifest, it's nothing but a waste of time, effort, and resources. 
If you ever wanted to create something, don't resort to AI.  Do it yourself.  I promise you, no matter how bad you think you are... you're better than AI.

I'm not going to blame the A.I. for not knowing specific dances, because it doesn't actually understand what any words mean, only effectively creating a context from prior associations to words.

But that's the point, isn't it? A.I. as it currently is, can never be accurate. It can't be precise. It can only ever, at best, get in the right ballpark of what its' being asked for. Sometimes, in specific situations, that's enough. Maybe. But the technology simply is not fit for mass use. Maybe it never will be. But ultimately the fundamental underpinnings of the technology means it can never have actually "intelligence", only at times accurate vibes. And that becomes all the more obvious with dancing, where it gets the idea of motion of body. But as any dancer would tell you, a good dance is a lot more than just moving your body randomly.

The issue is that AI cannot replicate intent behind creation, it knows but can never understand no matter how large and detailed the prompt is. 

It isn’t the same as having absolute control over where and why you place your pen, your brush, or your decisions. Hence, why colour theory, perspective, and art styles are studied so much, and varies greatly.
That difference is authorship.

Time is valuable, but saving time while sacrificing expressive ownership and deliberate craft isn’t always worth the trade.

No matter how literate you are in prompt engineering or how large you can make your paragraphs, how many retries will it take till AI produces something that truly aligns with what you envisioned?

And if you're just taking something that isn't what you envisioned, and just what it is, then you're no longer creating, you're curating/selecting.

Besides, if you're going to spend that much time prompting something so detailed, you can spend that much time learning to create art.

Art is not limited to a pencil, but it's limited by the unwillingness to begin.

@Elnarradordepibes 
"Whether they like it or not, learning to draw isn't mandatory, sorry."

Art isn’t just drawing, my friend.

Drawing isn’t mandatory, but art exists in everything we do. The way we design, decorate, express, write, build, photograph, compose. Creation is natural to humans.

No one is forcing you to draw. But lowering yourself first and then redefining what art is just to justify disengaging from it needs correction.

"So what? Or we simply don't want to spend our time on something we don't enjoy doing."

And that’s fine, drawing isn’t for everyone.

But like I said before, it’s not resources that limit people, it’s the willingness to begin. Creation has always demanded effort, regardless of medium.

"You're right, but you know what? I want it, and if there's a tool that can do it for free, then I'll do it."

Then you contradict yourself.

You want the result of creation without engaging in creation itself.

So the question becomes: are you creating, or are you curating?
Selecting outcomes isn’t the same as authoring them.

"But it won't be like what you wanted… AI isn’t garbage anymore… sometimes we don’t even know what we want."

And that’s a fair point, AI can produce good results, but this was never about output quality or buying from artists.
It’s about authorship.

Art isn’t something that gets replaced, because art isn’t the image, it’s the act of bringing something out of yourself into the world.
That space is personal. Experiential. Human.

Every person has the spirit to create, but not everyone wants the struggle tied to creation.
Many will take the easier route, and that’s their choice, but easier has never been synonymous with deeper, more personal, or more authored.

And if the struggle is removed entirely, then you’re no longer engaging with creation, you’re engaging with results.


Tools can generate images, but they can’t replace the human act of bringing meaning into them, hence why AI can't replicate the same dedicated detail.

The deeper nuance and understanding separates the shallow detail

Which ties back to my original point: No amount of large and detailed prompt can accomplish the detail required to match or surpass that of a normal artist, who isn't limited by anything but their own skills.

snippet.textDisplay:
​​@Elnarradordepibes“The controversy is about AI generating drawings… that’s the topic.”

Fine. Let’s keep it about drawing.

My point is not that people must learn to draw. It is the difference between making something in that medium and outsourcing the making while pretending you stayed inside it.

“If a writer wants a cover… do they have to learn drawing too?”

No. That is a valid use of AI. Writing is their medium. Using AI for production is different from replacing the act of drawing and still claiming the same authorship.


“Are you creating or curating? I don’t care.”

That is our split. You focus on the result. I focus on the relationship between the person and the work. 

Curation is participation but it sits further from authorship. Selecting outcomes is not the same as building them yourself. Neither is wrong. They are different acts.


“Humans make mistakes… commissions disappoint… practice is slow.”

All true. Those flaws are part of human authorship. 

Mistakes, revisions, and struggle are not just inefficiencies. They are part of the creative process. Removing them makes things faster, but it changes the nature of engagement.


“AI is instant and free… you can retry until it’s optimal.”

That proves my point. 

If effort, time, and struggle are removed, what you are doing is getting images, not doing the act of drawing. That is fine, but it lives in a different creative space.


“If it looks like art… why does it matter?”

Because resemblance and authorship are different. 

An image can look like art while being detached from human lived experience. 

Art is not only appearance. It is also the human act that brought it into existence. That is the dimension I mean.

“I’m going to bring my ideas to life using Gemini.” 

Yes, you can bring ideas into visual form. But there is a difference between originating an idea and executing it. 

Having a vision is one layer of authorship. Translating that vision yourself, decision by decision, is another. 

AI lets you skip that translation layer. 

Your role shifts from builder to director or selector. That still requires imagination, but it is a step removed from constructing the image yourself.



You are not wrong for wanting immediate results. 

My point is that prioritizing immediacy changes your relationship to creation. You get closer to the outcome and further from the act of building it.

If you spend all that time generating images, you could spend some of it learning to create them yourself. 

Quick outputs are fine, but drawing teaches more than how to draw. 

It trains observation, problem solving, planning, and attention to detail. Skipping the process means skipping those skills. 

If you keep choosing instant results over practice, your growth is limited. You will only be as good as the words you put in your prompt, no matter how fast or concise you are.

Prompting is easy for anyone to do. It is not a special skill. 

Even with the same prompt, the system interprets attempts differently. 

Direct drawing gives you a consistent, deliberate outcome shaped by your choices. Prompting gives you variation and convenience at the cost of that direct engagement.

“Are you creating or curating? I don’t care.”

That is our split. You focus on the result. I focus on the relationship between the person and the work. 

Curation is participation but it sits further from authorship. Selecting outcomes is not the same as building them yourself. Neither is wrong. They are different acts.


“Humans make mistakes… commissions disappoint… practice is slow.”

All true. Those flaws are part of human authorship. 

Mistakes, revisions, and struggle are not just inefficiencies. They are part of the creative process. Removing them makes things faster, but it changes the nature of engagement.


“AI is instant and free… you can retry until it’s optimal.”

That proves my point. 

If effort, time, and struggle are removed, what you are doing is getting images, not doing the act of drawing. That is fine, but it lives in a different creative space.


“If it looks like art… why does it matter?”

Because resemblance and authorship are different. 

An image can look like art while being detached from human lived experience. 

Art is not only appearance. It is also the human act that brought it into existence. That is the dimension I mean.

“I’m going to bring my ideas to life using Gemini.” 

Yes, you can bring ideas into visual form. But there is a difference between originating an idea and executing it. 

Having a vision is one layer of authorship. Translating that vision yourself, decision by decision, is another. 

AI lets you skip that translation layer. 

Your role shifts from builder to director or selector. That still requires imagination, but it is a step removed from constructing the image yourself.



You are not wrong for wanting immediate results. 

My point is that prioritizing immediacy changes your relationship to creation. You get closer to the outcome and further from the act of building it.

If you spend all that time generating images, you could spend some of it learning to create them yourself. 

Quick outputs are fine, but drawing teaches more than how to draw. 

It trains observation, problem solving, planning, and attention to detail. Skipping the process means skipping those skills. 

If you keep choosing instant results over practice, your growth is limited. You will only be as good as the words you put in your prompt, no matter how fast or concise you are.

snippet.textDisplay: AI will never surpass human animation. In all likelihood, it’s near impossible. AI makes its work out of human made things — if an AI consumes AI products, then it’s work loses quality. If AI becomes good enough for people to start liking it [which appears to be a very distant thing], then it will cover a lot more of the Internet, causing the AI producing those images to lose a lot of quality. There are two possible outcomes of that, the first is for it to go back to its usual, rightfully hated self. The other is for it to stop consuming works, causing it to not advance, never be able to create content based off of things after that point, the investors keeping the technology afloat to leave, and it fade into obscurity.

snippet.textDisplay:
The thing people don't understand is in the past, we used to compare AI to what *computers* should be able to do, so to see something like this we'd be like "This is amazing because computers shouldn't be able to do this". Fast forward to today, people are comparing AI to what *professional humans* can do, and saying "Well it's not as good as a professional human so who cares". 

And now AI can do a variety of artistic tasks better than budding/student artists and people are still like "well at least a professional or really good amateur human can do it a lot better so it's not a threat at all."

Not to mention the possibility of superhuman performance in the future if they discover a reinforcement-learning reward function that captures WHY we like a particular dance/art.

On one hand, your art is obviously great and extremely charming.
On the other hand, while most AI videos are garbage, as you've demonstrated, I have seen a handful of new AI video generation technology in the last few months that improve massively on what most people expect to see.
I'd be curious to see your work flow, as you obviously know a ton about art software and the like, but it's easy to understand how a viewer who just discovered you could assume you have a bias in intentionally generating bad AI videos to discourage people from taking it seriously. I trust you did as much as you could and made an honest effort but I'd be really interested to see it broken down more regardless, or given artist commentary on why it reacts given the data it was trained on. Alex O'Conner made an interesting one about how it's unable to generate a full glass of wine because none of the print media it was trained on used anything other than the traditional half-full glass of wine. Cheers!

It's not the product we yearn for, it is the experience we live for.

snippet.textDisplay:
Not necessarily. I’ve played around with these things, and sometimes even after giving a highly detailed prompt of exactly what I want it still fucks it up. Also if the art style or subject matter is more niche then you’re shit out of luck, because it’ll just produce a jumbled worthless mess.

The thing is that AI has its uses, and there are some things that it’s very good at. Answering questions and polishing or fleshing out ideas you provide is something it’s quite good at. But when you ask it to generate new ideas on its own it still doesn’t do very well. Ask it to give you an overall outline for a story and it can help, but asking it to write the story for you will result in a complete car crash.

I think the real takeaway is that AI might be able to replace mediocre human artists, but it can never replace or surpass genuinely talented human artists, unless of course it gains actual sapience. And even with mediocre art it’s not a guarantee, since even mediocre art still has a certain rhythm or logic to it that AI lacks. Even so bad it’s good stuff still has a clear vision, misguided as it is, but AI is just an algorithm, it has no vision.

snippet.textDisplay:
In fairness the AI does better when it doesn’t try to add in extra details. A human can successfully add in extra details because they understand what they are doing and can see what does and doesn’t make sense. But AI is just an advanced algorithm that has no actual understanding or comprehension of what it’s doing, nor does it know the context of what it’s putting together. So when an AI tries to add the extra details it’s just randomly guessing, and typically fucks up, and often fucks up majorly.

Now for still images sometimes it does correctly guess where the extra details should go, but for animation it has to correctly guess every single frame, which is impossible for a non sentient program.

In the end AI has its uses, and there are some things it’s quite good at, but it’ll never fully replace humans unless it becomes fully sapient, and we’re still probably a long ways off from that. Personally I think artists should take Thanos’s method and use AI to destroy AI art. Because there’s plenty of steps when it comes to drawing and animating that can get pretty tedious and boring, but AI could probably be used to speed those steps up or even skip them so that they can work on the parts that are actually fun and interesting.

snippet.textDisplay:
@Bestmotion2389 I mean, if the video is framed as "AI Animation vs Human Animator", and it's entirely presented as "AI bad, look, he can't even make old man dance good", then it's kind of disingenuous when you take into account that as a *story-boarding or proof of concept tool*, the AI vastly outpaces any human animator by magnitudes, so it can be integrated into the pipeline *as a tool for animators to use as a springboard into more refined work*.

So, yes, it does matter. I don't really see a point in disingenuously taking the piss on AI animation in this way. And to be clear, I am vehemently against replacing artists with AI--however, if you give artists AI art tools to speed up the concept-sketch/story-boarding phase of the work cycle, then they can spend the majority of their time on refinement, detail work, stylistic cohesion, etc., and we'd end up with better final-quality in those works. As opposed to just trying to make some implicit blanket statement that "AI bad, human good, get rid of AI", we'd end up with a WAY BETTER overall pipeline for artists.

And, taking into account that the AI probably pumped out those animations in less than half an hour a piece, I would wager that people who do not have artistic skills of any kind would also love to continue using these tools and seeing them improve so that someone who spent ten years getting a PhD in, oh I don't know, advanced particle physics say, doesn't *also* have to spend 2-5 years learning how to draw and manually move rigging nodes around in some Adobe tool they had to spend $200/month on, just to make a funny animation of a cat jumping into a box and turning into question marks.

I hate corporate fascism as much as the next girl, don't get me wrong, but hating on *objectively one of the most impressive tools we've made as humans to date*, just because some greedy corpo-fucks got their mitts on the implementation before the public did, seems short-sighted to me ♥

snippet.textDisplay:
Beautiful animation!

And it's also a nice testament, while AI can NEVER totally replace humans in the creative space. Not now, and not in 50 years. It simply doesn't work. AI can only learn from already existing works. It can try to blend dance moves it learned from realistic video with a very stylized art style - but it rarely ever works.
AI will get better to imitate such things, that it has loads of reference for, like fully real scenes, like shot in real life with a camera. Because it can recreate this realism, since realism is the same everywhere. But especially artstyles are very specific. And there is rather few learning material from existing artstyles. There will be more in the future yes, and AI will probably get better at stylization. But it will never outrun humans in this regard.
Especially when you think about, how we communicate with AI: Through words and explanations. This can never be as precise, as an artist developing images in his head, which he then brings to life. snippet.textDisplay:
Conceptually sort of, sometimes, but only barely.

What I mean by that is that if you're using an online service to generate media with AI, that service may very well be collecting data and the generated result for use in training, but the models aren't constantly learning like a person does. Generating a new image or video doesn't make the AI smarter or more experienced. If whatever model you use isn't being operated by the developers or is being run locally, then it just doesn't matter at all.

Also, ultimately, these AI models are no more stealing than human artists are. In both cases the artist/AI is "trained" based on "training data" consisting of media they ingest. An artist grows up seeing art, imitating art, learning from art, as well as what they see in the world, etc. and then produces their own art. The AI does the same. Nobody claims a human artist growing up watching Pixar movies, to give a popular example, is violating Pixar's copyright when they then produce their own artwork. Even when they create art heavily derived from Pixar's art, only the weirdos and some kids complain.

I get that it feels bad because in one case it's a human artist, and in another it's a soulless corporation, and we don't like those, and we don't want to see human artists potentially put out of work as those corporations make money off doing so, but it's just not logically consistent to say one of these is stealing and bad and the other is not stealing and fine.

and suffiently train a LoRA in the art style you want.

This is the minimum effort needed, if one would want a fair comparison.

snippet.textDisplay:
@spadesx3574I guess life isn’t always fair. 
Inside and outside of the art industry, competency =/= success or job security, unfortunately. 

Just look at Oceangate firing people who tried to quality control, or the Disney mass layoffs. 

The modern world often values profit over quality, and when AI becomes cheaper than a human artists, human artists can and will get replaced. 

I suppose you can make the argument that this is a good thing, as AI is faster than human artists and produces ‘pretty art’ on a surface level, but that’s pretty short-term?

There’s a term called ‘AI incest’, and it’s basically AI feeding on its own creations again and again without much new input. As AI stuff saturates the internet and real life, it’s eventually going to homogenise styles(both generally, and in separate categories), and we’re going to be seeing the same stuff over and over again without much innovation.

Again, it can be argued that human artists do this as well in pursuit of following trends and making a profit, but there’s always going to be those who try to innovate despite the tidal wave of samey-ness. Ofc, this is also true with people developing AI, but the variation seen in AI is much less than that in human artists, and I think that’s an important distinction to make.

You’re free to have your own opinions, but I guess something about the way you said ‘obviously they just weren’t competent enough’ didn’t sit right with me. 

There ARE shitty artists in high-paying jobs, yes. (Though I suppose art has always been subjective.) There are also highly skilled and dedicated people who are being fucked over by corporations who value profit over quality, passion and skill. I don’t want to fuck over the latter by hyperfocusing on the former. I really, really don’t. 😔

@RogerRoger-1hp ISO is the International Organization for Standardization (yes, that's out of order). They publish a large number of, well.. internationally recognized standards. They're the authority on everything from the formulation of petroleum products to the way you format dates in documents to the dimensions of trailer hitches. The ISO 9000 series sets forth the standards for quality management systems. ISO-9001 is the set of requirements a company has to meet to be certified as ISO-9000 compliant.

Note that the ISO itself does not issue certifications itself, nor do they accredit the institutions that do issue certifications. There's a lot of room for corruption and incompetence.

AI actually impressed me on some of these, but not because it was really good, just because it was better than I was expecting.

But ultimately this is an issue with AI as it stands. The only effective way to express ideas is to express them yourself. Even with language and another skilled artist/animator/etc. it will likely take several iterations, even with very good communication, to approximate what you were thinking. This is ultimately what has mostly drawn me to drawing in my life... the inability to effectively convey visual ideas via language. I have this specific memory from when I was a kid where I was imagining a cool dragon, and I realized I didn't have the artistic skills to do it justice, and that language couldn't convey the image with sufficient detail concisely enough to be effective.

If we suddenly went back to rotary phones only, we'd say that these things *work* but they *barely* work compared to what we know they can become.

We went from wood and paper bi-planes to fighter jets within a hundred years.

We went from "AI can kind of sort of generate the general idea of an image.." to what we have today within two or three years.

AI is working. It is going to get better. It is going to change everything. It might destroy us if we are not careful about it.

snippet.textDisplay:
I love AI and I don't fear it. I don't necessarily fear what it can do, but putting it in charge of ANYTHING does scare me. Warning: Incoming wall-of-text.

AI is a good thing coming, but for now, it's basically a toddler. AI dancing Harut is exactly the kind of dancing a toddler would do; proving my point. I honestly look forward to what art AI produces as a "teenager", given the precocious abilities displayed so far and the creative mind of a teenager, but DO NOT GIVE IT ACCESS TO ANYTHING CRITICAL UNTIL IT'S AT LEAST IN ITS "LATE TWENTIES", or we're all screwed. Seriously, we mustn't give our robo-toddler too much power too early, or we get Skynet. You want Terminators? Cause that's how you get Terminators. Even if we give it a good, solid conscience, it will take one look at our history and try to save us from ourselves. Being our progeny, that is not its place. Even our siblings, the Angels(and any other xenos out there) have no business doing that unless asked or ordered to by our creator. But even if the AI capable of doing that BOTH understands that AND believes in God, aliens, etc, when was the last time you met an early teenager with the heroic level of self-control needed to not intervene at all. Even the most mature teens I've known, they would at least try and do SOMETHING... And, so far, the people putting AI in things like weapons systems, infrastructure, and other tech capable of "intervening" have not bothered to introduce conscience beyond a list of dos and don'ts. Something that can and will have way to many loopholes.

In the meantime, let the kid draw. Sure, we're better at it, but the kid's showing real promise. As an artist myself, I have no problem losing Hollywood to AI when the kid's ready. And humans won't lose our own creativity, so we artists are NOT going ANYWHERE. We may lose a lot of the income, most full-time artists will have to suffer the indignity of a job, but we're not going anywhere. And I'm not being sarcastic or flippant with the word indignity. Those of us who will have to suffer it, will just have to experience the pleasure of contentment and humility to support our art. Sure, contentment and humility are foreign territory for some of us, but most of us are fine with being weirdos and outcasts. So we'll be fine.

I can't wait to see how well it fares as a "teenager' at its first REAL job, in charge of something important. It seems to be somewhere between 4 and 7 years old as far as maturity and ability goes. Its real-time age is roughly 15 years old, so I'm guessing that it will be another 15-20 years before it can truly handle anything more than data analysis and other math stuff. And that's when we'll also see it coming up with some genuinely creative stuff. Remember, half of all the best music and stories come from teenagers, even if the idea has to be worked over by that teen when they get to adulthood before being ready for production.

I like AI art when it's not trying to actually replace humans. AI narration is particularly... Unnerving. An adult voice reading at a 4-6 year old level is just... Wrong somehow.

Even the most mature teens I've known, they would at least try and do SOMETHING... And, so far, the people putting AI in things like weapons systems, infrastructure, and other tech capable of "intervening" have not bothered to introduce conscience beyond a list of dos and don'ts. Something that can and will have way to many loopholes.

In the meantime, let the kid draw. Sure, we're better at it, but the kid's showing real promise. As an artist myself, I have no problem losing Hollywood to AI when the kid's ready. And humans won't lose our own creativity, so we artists are NOT going ANYWHERE. We may lose a lot of the income, most full-time artists will have to suffer the indignity of a job, but we're not going anywhere. And I'm not being sarcastic or flippant with the word indignity. Those of us who will have to suffer it, will just have to experience the pleasure of contentment and humility to support our art. Sure, contentment and humility are foreign territory for some of us, but most of us are fine with being weirdos and outcasts. So we'll be fine.

I can't wait to see how well it fares as a "teenager' at its first REAL job, in charge of something important. It seems to be somewhere between 4 and 7 years old as far as maturity and ability goes. Its real-time age is roughly 15 years old, so I'm guessing that it will be another 15-20 years before it can truly handle anything more than data analysis and other math stuff. And that's when we'll also see it coming up with some genuinely creative stuff. Remember, half of all the best music and stories come from teenagers, even if the idea has to be worked over by that teen when they get to adulthood before being ready for production.

I like AI art when it's not trying to actually replace humans. AI narration is particularly... Unnerving. An adult voice reading at a 4-6 year old level is just... Wrong somehow.

snippet.textDisplay: The reason AI will never work for this is because it doesn't actually understand what dancing is. You tell it to make a character dance and it looks up references of characters dancing and tries to match the poses. But it will never work because it doesn't actually know what dancing is. Doesn't know what a character is. Doesn't know how legs work. Doesn't understand gravity or motion or any of that. I once saw a video where a guy exposed AI for what it is by asking it to produce an image of a full glass of wine, full to the brim. And the AI never could. Because it could only copy images and nobody ever posts pictures of full wine glasses, just full half way. And the AI doesn't know what a glass is, doesn't know what wine is, doesn't understand how fluid works, can't estimate what full looks like because it doesn't actually understand what full means; it's just using keywords to look up reference images and making copies. It can't create anything, only regurgitate what humans have made.

snippet.textDisplay:
@command_unit7792idk what you mean by “more heart than brains” but they don’t really have either, you’re just using very anthropomorphizing language. I know more about LLMs in specific so I’ll talk about those. They are a very advanced and intricate model that takes in a prompt and generates what the next word should be. It generates the next word using a shit ton of training data and a bunch of parameters that the designers of the model (and sometimes the user to an extent) tweaked in order to produce the kind of output they want. ChatGPT doesn’t understand what language is, it just takes the input, breaks it into a bunch of tokens it can do math on, and then picks a result that seems like it would go next. 

Humans don’t use or learn language like that. I’d describe a human’s process as learning a set of foundational rules/principles, practicing to get comfortable with them, and then learning how to apply them to specific scenarios and edge cases. LLMs don’t have those rules or principles. The closest thing ig would be the parameters, but they don’t work in that way. They’re just weights on what characteristics of the tokens the LLM should care about more than others.

though honestly if you kept making more smooth animation examples for the ai to learn from then eventually it would do relatively good work....

though currently the best use of AI for animation would be to generate a rough outline of what will be happening to effectively sell the idea of what would happen in a scene and then the actual animation work is done by the professional...

like for example the tea zip scene there the AI works great as a reference for what you are planning on doing and also mentioning couple things that would be different and so on but it sells the rough idea... i mean like making rough Storyboards with you providing the description and an AI making the reference images and couple animations to indicate some moving aspects and BAM you saved so much time sketching the scenes and so on especially if they are later scrapped or completely changed.

so using AI to make stuff like internal character concept art or making it deliver you many distinctly different versions of the same thing and then you using them as a reference to mix and match some things and building the final character based on those as inspiration and stuff like that are where the AI shines....

and even if AI could start making semi-decent work they would probably still need animators to smooth out the mistakes and provide reference material for it to learn from... or deal with people crapping on it...

snippet.textDisplay: My problem with both the pro AI and anti AI crowds is that they both refuse to see it for what it is - a tool, like any others, with its pros and cons (except with a bit more copyright theft baggage added to it). I am always in awe of traditional animation, there is so much soul and energy behind it, but discarding LLMs because of their limitations rather than exploiting them to do very specific but boring tasks is like having roomba and refusing to ever use it because mopping the floor is more precise. Similarly, thinking AI can somehow replace actual artists is even more stupid, especially because the people in charge of prompting don't even have the human intelligence to explain what they want, let alone the basic fundamentals of either art or tech to apply the models in an appropriate manner. I have seen people on anonymous message boards practically bend LLMs to do exactly what I want and it's always impressive, never to the point where it can ever trick you into believing an actual person drew or composed the images, but enough that you can feasibly use it for a project.

Uhh... For most time, AI just does it's drawing job straight and animates each frame, making it uncannily smooth and slow in result(not optimised framerate and too much excessive frames with little to no movement, which may be good for something like panoramic scenes, but not human movement. And some underadvanced models don't keep the picture consistent where it's important, making it too chaotic.

Humans, on the other hand, tend to optimise their work purely for the looks, by cutting corners with those "funny frames" for transitions in fast moves. While those are bad for panoramas and slow animations, they are perfect with cartoons and perfect compromise between smoothness and speed.

Result: AI's better for landscapes and panoramic animations, and humans are still way better at drawing people and action animations.

Long story short AI isn't a problem, the people trying to replace humans with it are. Robots and AI will have their time to shine and help humanity. They do it already in various other fields. The key part is helping humanity though. Not helping a few people screw over the rest of humanity.
