snippet.textDisplay:
AI is an inevitability in art, sadly. I think it'll still be fundamental to have an actual artist though to wrangle the AI. You can see the AI struggles to do any kind of exaggerated, emotive movements. This is going to be a problem for anyone not skilled in animation or choreography because they won't have the practiced creativity or knowledge to get the AI to do what they're thinking of. 

I foresee AI basically replacing a lot of people's ability to be creative, improvise, or communicate abstract ideas through a medium. Anyone can punch in a prompt like "have them do the Cha Cha," but if you don't know how to utilize perspective, angles, contrast, color theory or lighting, it won't have any impact. 

I do metalworking and as advanced as the technology is, you still need to have an understanding of the fundamentals. A great example is CNC machining. The designer might be able to come up with the design file for the machine, but if they don't know what the limitations of the equipment is, the machine simply can't do what they need. For example, the designer might design a piece in the software that has an interior right angle, and you know, great, works in your file, but the machine can't bend around corner inside the material. There's also times where they design a piece that would have to be milled down from a giant block of steel, when an experienced machinist would know to just have the end product be a few different pieces.

snippet.textDisplay:
I'm not principally against AI, but this comparison/contrast really captures how modern major AI is poorly constructed, poorly trained, and poorly used.

snippet.textDisplay: The biggest reason AI animation is CENTURIES behind AI artworks is that art can be copied to SOME degree with formulaic learning. You can learn mathematic patterns on pixel-based rendering using references. You cannot reference many other animations, because frame-by-frame analysis would take PETABYTES of storage and libraries. Beyond that, it STILL wouldn't work properly, because it doesn't comprehend the principles of animation like Hayk here does. Squash and stretch, breaking the form, purposefully going off model for emphasis. Harut was stretching that leg to almost 40% longer its original length, but it was to emphasize the slide-steps and SMOOTHNESS! Jiggles happen on beats and with movement. There are things that require expression, things that are MUCH MUCH HARDER to mathematically quantify, ESPECIALLY when you start considering that you have to render them from other angles. We're still safe for now, and probably for the next 30 years at least.

snippet.textDisplay:
Can't help but think of an AI discussion vid I've seen from another animator named Toniko Pantoja when seeing this. He was probably the first guy I've seen who didn't necessarily dismiss AI on the basis of it being "stolen work", but it's moreso just the fact that the tool's just TOO streamlined/universal in general for it to really mean much. Like, someone could grab an AI and tell it to make something, but in the process they basically just completely skip the rest of what's involved in art. Which is to say, all the effort, struggle, and time it takes to slowly refine one's craft, learn themselves 'n their strengths/weaknesses, and basically evolve as a person to a point where one can accomplish a particular idea the way they want to, really just isn't there one bit when you use AI to try and make stuff.

It's like, sure, sometimes it makes some cool looking things, but at the end of the day it's just completely and utterly meaningless. No satisfaction, no self-growth, just a product so devoid of story that the only folks who think it's worth much are those who are essentially incapable of understanding what it means to improve and put love into something to begin with, if that makes sense. And well, I guess maybe also has a tiny bit of value to those who find it funny (because tbh, 'sometimes' there's funny AI memes and noises out there), but comedic-based content like that is still just a basic one-off gag that doesn't really stick around as well as most other hand-crafted memes to begin with.

I'm probably not doing his video on the topic proper justice as this is really just an abbreviated interpretation of the content, but I reckon that's still a good perspective to have because it's the most blunt and objectively true interpretation of what it means (or well, the lack of real meaning, because at the end of the day it's literally just a shoddy shortcut) to use AI. Also totally gonna recommend the lad either way because he's enough of a giga-chad to not just make animations, but fun tutorials/guides too, so yeh.

Making a static picture is something AI can do because it mostly relies on copying. And pattern recognition.

A foot or shoe should go here because its the end of a leg.

(This is also why it completely falls apart with non-standard character designs)

Actually animating movement however requires an understanding of biology. It requires intent, it requires an intuitive understanding of how much exaggeration you need and can get away with, etc.

While I have no doubt that someday we will have an AI that can do simple animations (like walk cycles): it won’t be achieved with this current model. And likely not in our lifetime.

I was impressed by how cohesive the AI was though. I was expecting it to be a lot worse.

It absolutely *pales* in comparison to your animations though. I would almost call the comparison unfair since you are probably better than the average animator that i’ve seen

The limbic system influences creation, so that memories, moods, and personal meanings are captured in strokes, colors, and shapes. At the same time, subjectivity causes each brain to select, filter, and interpret different details, projecting internal experiences and symbols. Therefore, two people standing in front of the same object produce different drawings: each reflects not only what is seen, but also what the person drawing feels and means.

I want to look at art and feel like I KNOW the artist. I want a sense that there are still humans with personalities, just like me. I want to feel something. A struggle or a euphoria someone went through, or just simple goofy feelings before they made the art. What has AI gone through? Lagging, obeying, mashing things together, sucking plugs, and trying to IMITATE life. Honestly answer me this: Why on earth would you want to see something that wasn’t made by a living being, besides just for stimulation?

Also AI is really bad for the environment because it makes the computer overwork, using water to cool itself down, meaning that there’s a bit less water every time AI is used. If this keeps up for like 100 years, the Great Lakes will turn into the Decent Puddles, the Red Sea will turn into the Brown Pond, and the Pacific Ocean will turn into the Pathetic Lake.

Basically, this was a world made for living beings. We’re supposed to do and make things for each other. I doubt that life’s purpose was for us to see a bunch of inanimate, non-living computers live amongst themselves.

⁠@sirosterthetoaster I agree that AI will probably never have emotions, and we can use the word 'never' when discussing their lack of feelings. AI-generated art will likely never be worth as much as human art if we consider real art to involve emotions in the process, as a way to express our emotions. However, some people don't put emotions into their art, and I don't either. I don't even understand how to infuse emotions into my artwork; it's mostly a simple replica of what I see or imagine. This might be why art isn't a passion for me; it's not an identity, just a capacity. I see art as a tool, an advantage I have. I'm still proud when I create something because it's proof of my capacity, and I enjoy it when people are impressed. That's it. When I use AI to generate something, it's like taking a random picture or image from the internet. I can enjoy the result, love it, and use it, but I won't be proud of something I didn't create.

According to this definition, my artwork doesn't hold more value than an AI-generated image because there's no emotional charge in it. It's easy to claim, "I put emotions into it" when we didn't, it's not something we can see or prove. For someone interested in the final results, whether it's AI or human-made it doesn't matter. If there are enough people who value results over process and emotions, it's only a matter of time before AI replaces artists.

What I dislike is reasoning based on hopes, emotions, and beliefs rather than critical thinking and facts. Saying that AI will never replace humans doesn't sound very neutral or realistic; it sounds like an emotional discharge driven by hopes and beliefs rather than critical thoughts based on facts. It's a fact that machines and technology have replaced humans more and more over time, and this is a historical reality. People will get used to AI and normalize its use, just as they have with every novelty and new technology. There's always resistance, and I dislike this because I feel like history is repeating itself, with the same close-minded people resisting progress.

If people were completely rational, I'd be fine with this resistance. However, I'm afraid it's mostly driven by insecurities rather than a realistic estimation. I don't see any apocalyptic or real-life threats right now. People have always been against novelty – microwaves are dangerous, electricity is dangerous, cars are dangerous – and this pattern will likely continue with AI. It's true that these technologies can be dangerous, but their pros outweigh their cons, and everyone uses them today without questioning it.

I'm afraid it's the same with AI, and this is what irritates me. If only people were completely rational. All I see is people being insecure about purely emotional stuff – fear of being replaced, fear of being useless, fear of losing their identity. I don't see any actual life-threatening issues. I'm afraid that those who say "AI will never be good at making music" would love an AI-generated song if they didn't know it was created by AI, but would suddenly dislike it if they were told. This clearly shows bias, and it's what irritates me. I see this as a lack of mental strength.

If people enjoy music for its results and don't care about emotions or projecting their own emotions into it, the same fate awaits them as visual artists. I do consider the cons of AI – they have ecological impacts, can be wrong, and could lead to more radical and unpredictable changes than other technologies. The world could become more controlled and monitored, with people relying too heavily on AI and losing their ability to think critically. However, there are also positive sides to AI, but I'm not going to list them here.

I'm not pro-AI or anti-AI; I'm critical of everything and support or reject ideas based on logical reasoning and facts. I can change my mind in a second if there's any logical dissonance. There's no camp, no ego to defend – just logical reasoning and facts. I'm talking about subtle psychology, where people think they're objective in their reasoning when they're subtly influenced by their emotions, hopes, and beliefs instead of being completely honest with themselves – aka the illusion of objectivity bias.

snippet.textDisplay:
@okasan-vk8jo it would still be AI. Its artificial, and has intelligence. Thats what AI is. How intelligent is irrelevant, even if its just as capable or even more so than humans.


Also, Quote[The reason AI cant replace anything because it cant generate anything on its own.....]

This is just false. AI is perfectly capable of generating things on it's own. And does so all the time. You mistake this with the idea of being able to create art humans think looks good without human input. AI needs human input to know what art humans like, by definition, because this isnt a just a constant fact of the universe, its a subjective thing.

AI can only do things which have a well defined goal. And for making art, the only way to GIVE it a well defined goal, is by showing it examples of what humans think make good art. AI is perfectly capable of making it's own "art". Its just that humans wouldnt find it appealing, because there is no built in fact of the universe that says this art is good or this art isnt. So AI is perfectly capable of generating random noise and calling that art, but that isnt what humans specifically like. If AI wants to create art that humans like, it's going to need human input on what humans actually like.


Its akin to you trying to make art that an intelligent alien species would like, that has tastes COMPLETELY different from that of humans. The only way possible to know what kind of art this alien species likes, is by getting direct feedback. Either by trying to mimic examples of their art that they provide you, OR by getting feedback on if the art you make is to their liking or not. But no matter what, you need the feedback of that alien species to know if the art you make is to their tastes or not. Without their feedback, you can never make "art" that they would approve of consistently. And its the same for an AI. They dont share the same subjective aesthetic value of art humans do, so the ONLY WAY for them to know what kind of art humans like, is with human feedback. Its not that they are incapable of generating stuff on their own, its that they are incapable of generating art HUMANS like without HUMAN feedback. Because thats always how it is with subjective things.



Quote[But lets say an AI has ALL those human feature, Can you still call it a simple AI? ]

Call it an AI? Absolutely. Call it a SIMPLE AI? No. Its not a simple AI anymore, but it is still an AI.

And in fact, it's an AGI, which is a very special terminology resolved for very specific AI, which do not currently exist. AGI are much more similar to humans in that they exhibit general intelligence. General intelligence is the ability to learn more than just what you were specifically designed to do. Its a little more complicated than that, but thats the general jist. 


In order to actually properly behave like a human, AI must at LEAST already be AGI level intelligences. And ANY AGI is already significantly world changing, and categorically different from more simple AI. But they ARE still AI at the end of the day. Just a different category of AI.

Also, there is no universal law that makes AGI behave like humans either. In fact, its pretty likely they wont. While it IS possible to make one that would behave like a human, its far more likely the first AGI wont. Humans behave the way we do because of millions of years of evolution causing us to be social creatures and empathetic and stuff. AGI will behave the way they do because of whatever reward function dictates their behavior. Which is unlikely to include human empathy. Not that it theoretically cant, its just unlikely to. But that will cause it to be just as intelligent as humans (and likely significantly more so), but also not behave like humans, or share our same desires.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@dogerianI understand your defense of human art, and it's a valid emotional response. This shift has happened again and again, and it's always society that decides.

Think of it this way: There's also art in pottery, textiles, potterya and tableware, but everything follows a path of "optimization", and even in music...

Actually, in music, we have one of the clearest examples: A master luthier spends months building a violin that costs $20,000. Yamaha, using automated processes, produces a violin of excellent and consistent quality for $500. The vast majority of students, schools, and even professional orchestras use these factory-made instruments because they are accessible and reliable.

In each case, the "soul" of the handmade item wasn't lost, but it became a niche. Society, through its everyday purchases, voted for accessibility, consistency, and affordability.

AI art is following the exact same path. It's not about replacing the human spirit... it's about democratizing creation, just as the mechanical loom democratized clothing. The market will ultimately decide its place, just as it always has...

snippet.textDisplay: @boeos9427 I apologize for my response before. Let me leave my emotional standpoint aside so I can be more clear. I agree with the statement that optimization is necessary for manufacturing and producing consistent copies of a product or piece. The manufacturing process becomes the art/artist itself in a way because the human touch is definitely not lost here. Through quality control and all the time that is saved, the artist/manufacturer can perfect other aspects of that product or piece that can ultimately unlock new standards of excellence while using less resources. Modern infrastructure and modern society itself just wouldn't be possible without this fact. Imagine if every repetitive mundane task absolutely had to be done by human hands alone... Not a world I'd like to live in that's for sure. I've seen and do respect real artists who use AI as a tool to assist them so that their true expertise can be focused on other aspects of their work, and ultimately reach new heights as an artist. HOWEVER... Once AI is no longer used as a tool, and is instead used to replace the artist altogether nothing good can come from it. I think in a way its misleading to say that AI even "generates'" anything at all. It's more of a regurgitation from an advanced algorithm that has sifted though and categorized most of available human art and knowledge in a very short time relatively speaking. If hundreds of years of human art didn't already exist to train these AI models,  it wouldn't have anything to regurgitate or "generate". The only reason a lot of AI generated art can seem "new" or "original" at all is because there's no way for a single human to become familiar with even a tiny fraction of the data AI was trained on and is regurgitating at them. So about 50% robotic. Lot of people in there doing work.
I don't see much that's really faster in that, and the number of people and the equipment cost means that it's only plausible as a highly subsidized business built on the idea that it will be able to perform long enough to cover the costs. As yet I don't think there are any companies that have paid off the automation costs, and are really looking at another decade or more before breaking even. That said, I can't wait for the robots. People, and this includes the programmers and engineers, just aren't interested for the most part, and that means they can't do a good job. These modular buildings simplify everything by turning it all into easily repeatable blocks.

I can build faster even with a group of half-trained people if I don't have to wait for inspections. But the automated parts are more precise than most carpenters can achieve.

snippet.textDisplay: The real exciting future I see is NOT factories with automation on processed Lumber.  It's In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) that mimics the way nature works  using local waste, byproducts and on-site soil/sand/concrete to create new materials and polymers to PRINT naturally strong shapes that do not need be screwed together or even painted.    Quantum computers will figure out the materials and formulas.  Very strong, agile and dexterous swarms of robots onsite will process and print on site.   The house of the future looks more like a conch shell than a home depot shed.  And nothing had to be shipped half way around the world to build it.  What we are going to need is power and a lot of it so I likely small and mobile nuclear power plants will be in our future.

snippet.textDisplay:
Apply this in Canada, and you will find it won't work; we have cold winters and need to lay a proper foundation below the frost line. The distances between assembly plants and job sites are a significant issue.
This is nothing more than a sales pitch, but in t reality the cost will be the same, or I think higher!
Every city above 100000 must have a plant, which will cost $ $ $ $ $. Every 3 days, a prefab home will be transported to the site and the parts assembled. 
The boxes will be ready; no roof, no finish, no cabinet work, no installation with heavy, expensive cranes. 
The production of 2 houses weekly, 40% complete, with the other 60% of work done on site development and finishing the home. 
In Canada, winter must be included in planning and will affect production!
These costly plants will produce about 230 homes a year.  
Having labour in the plant, transport, and placement with heavy equipment will be expensive. The window of construction will be from May to November, or 6 months, times 4 is 24 weeks, times 3 is 75 homes a year completed on site.
By prefabricating the partitions as a fold-down construction and transporting them to the site, it is much more effective and cheaper, and their planning and overhead are considerably lower. Factory-built homes have not been proven to be efficient and do not create higher volumes or save on labour or equipment. If it were cost-effective, builders would resort to this kind of production, but they have shown little or no interest! 
I have built several large prefabricated structures for office complexes, and they were effective because they were 3 stories tall and the walls were concrete elements with floors made out of prefab elements with 2'' poured concrete over top. It will take meticulous planning and scheduling; if not, it will be chaotic and lead to disaster.

Here is a clear and well-written American English translation of the text:
If we take Argentina’s continental surface area, which is 2,780,400 km², that is 2,780,400,000,000 square meters, and divide it by an estimated world population of 8.5 billion people, the result is that each person would be allocated approximately 327 square meters.
In other words, if the entire world population were physically placed within Argentina’s territory, every individual would have the equivalent of a reasonable urban lot. And even then, the rest of the planet would remain completely empty.
From this perspective, it is difficult to understand why a significant portion of humanity still lacks access to decent housing. From a purely physical and material standpoint, space is not the problem. Housing is not a technologically complex good either: its real cost should not, in many cases, exceed the price of a car.
Yet in practice, millions of dollars are paid for certain properties, and financial systems routinely offer 30-year (or longer) mortgages, a timeframe that often exceeds the actual lifespan of many of the materials used to build those homes.
Business is business, but when the broader picture is considered, a deep contradiction becomes evident: this is not an issue of space or resources, but rather one of economic structures, financial incentives, and social priorities. Seen this way, the current state of access to housing is not only inefficient—it borders on irrational.

snippet.textDisplay: The one step they missed in producing this home is that attic-foil should have been applied to the roof below the copper shingles. Since those shingles allow air to pass under them and upwards towards the crown, the attic-foil would create an infra-red barrier needed to keep the home cool in the summer, and warmer in the winter. Adding that to the roof adds minimal money spent versus years of HVAC costs. I used attic-foil in my attic space and it lowered my attic temp from 120°F-130°F to the ambient temperature outside (95°F). That 25°-35° difference cut my A/C bill in half every month!

snippet.textDisplay:
I know this technology looks promising and so on but in the past our grandfathers built houses with their own hands, love and joy. They harvested most of the materials in the nature. The whole process was very inspiring and accomplishing. You can't really compare the feeling to anything else when you step in the house you have built with love and passion for your family. When you live in such a hand built house you can feel every detail, every nuance, every imperfection. It has so much stories and life force in it. When robots build your house, your life also can become very robotistic, very repetitive, very routine. 
I am not saying it should be totally excluded, but simply to be aware of it. Surely it has it's own place in modern lifestyle and it may be perfect for some people, but if used improperly it can take away a whole dimension from a human life, a dimension which determine one's fulfillment by a very large degree, a dimension which determine what a human being really is.
Anyway, hats off to the people who built this technology, it is amazing to see something like that.

That's why this company is doing this. It's simply waiting for a buyout or is already using oligarch money to fund this.

This will NEVER lead to more affordable housing because, deep down, Americans don't want it. They want housing to basically be bitcoin. Nothing but a volatile investment.

snippet.textDisplay: Lots of wood used in the framing, thus high framing factor, thus significant thermal bridging. Wall to wall and wall to floor connections are not well air sealed. Volumetric modular to site means you're transporting a lot of air volume. Not efficient transportation. We use OSB in the U.S. and some say that's inferior to plywood, I saw what looks like particle board be used for sheathing! No air sealing of stud bays before inserting batt insulation. Batts are inferior to net and blow (blown in blanket) for insulation. Other techniques like framing bundles (ex: bmc ready-frame, or parr lumber's optiframe) is more efficient for the framing step.

I don't much care for their Lintels. 3- 2x's leaves no room for insulating and results in a Thermal Bridge (heat loss). When it's really cold out, there can be frost on the interior of the wall at the lintels. 
That said, it's a pretty amazing setup. There is a ton of money tied up in that Building and it's Robots. At least one doesn't have to worry about over-heating or freezing working outside (12 months of the year) but I'll take a hand-built home any day of the week. There was a Royal Homes pre-fab nearby me a few years ago. They didn't last long but for all I can remember, they might have gone under in 2008-09 Global Meltdown. 
But as a contractor and as a Chief Building Official, while there are many good things about Pre-Fab homes, there are several things that I didn't like about these structures. There is good and bad in everything though I guess. And again, the setup is still pretty impressive.

snippet.textDisplay:
Clickbait.  

Good video, but the title is a lie.  OK, so TECHNICALLY it is not a lie.  But to the question "Robots Build Houses Now?!", the answer is "No".

However, the thumbnail is totally a lie.  That never happens in the video,  There are never any robots at the home site.  And they never finish anything in the factory that size or to that degree of completion.  And nothing with that fancy design.  


Robots do some of the initial assembly, the workers finish building the rest and assemble it into sections.  Cranes and trucks bring it to the work site where cranes and workers assemble it.  No robots on the worksite.  The houses were built on the factory site, evidently for display purposes.  So, maybe it's just an experimental process so far?

And, the "Futuristic" in the title means pre-fab small houses a step up from trailer homes.

Then they tack another video onto the end about making a metal roof for a totally different structure.  Lot of manual work to make the tiles and a lot of manual work installing it.  No robots in that segment at all.

Why do they take a great video and ruin it with clickbait titles?

And I'd prefer no music to hear the ambient sounds of the machines and the work environment.  But, at least the music was inoffensive.
snippet.textOriginal:
Clickbait.  

Good video, but the title is a lie.  OK, so TECHNICALLY it is not a lie.  But to the question "Robots Build Houses Now?!", the answer is "No".

However, the thumbnail is totally a lie.  That never happens in the video,  There are never any robots at the home site.  And they never finish anything in the factory that size or to that degree of completion.  And nothing with that fancy design.  


Robots do some of the initial assembly, the workers finish building the rest and assemble it into sections.  Cranes and trucks bring it to the work site where cranes and workers assemble it.  No robots on the worksite.  The houses were built on the factory site, evidently for display purposes.  So, maybe it's just an experimental process so far?

And, the "Futuristic" in the title means pre-fab small houses a step up from trailer homes.

Then they tack another video onto the end about making a metal roof for a totally different structure.  Lot of manual work to make the tiles and a lot of manual work installing it.  No robots in that segment at all.

Why do they take a great video and ruin it with clickbait titles?

And I'd prefer no music to hear the ambient sounds of the machines and the work environment.  But, at least the music was inoffensive.

“What a deflection  avoiding the most vital question of all: will AI endanger us?”
There are scientists of integrity and conscience who have raised this concern with profound seriousness. The Gospel of Progress and the Hollow Throne
They call it the future.
A shining world of boundless intelligence, where machines dream and the young are told they are “the luckiest humans alive.”
But listen closer  beneath the gloss of promise hums a quieter truth.
The architects of this new Eden speak of destiny as if it were theirs to dictate, mistaking acceleration for awakening, and wealth for wisdom. They preach innovation while humanity itself drifts into abstraction.
The prophets of progress  men like Sam Altman  speak in circles that sound like revelation but ring hollow when pressed for meaning. They promise empowerment to a generation who cannot afford shelter. They conjure marvels, yet cannot speak of mercy.
GPT-3 to GPT-5  new skins on the same unexamined ghost.
Each model smarter, not kinder; faster, not wiser.
The myth of improvement masquerading as evolution.
Meanwhile, the living world waits  unseen, unheard.
AI creeps into the quiet work of doctors, teachers, poets, healers  the sacred labor of care and coherence. It does not yet know what it means to belong.
If I were twenty-two, I would not feel lucky.
I would feel haunted  standing at the threshold of a machine-made dawn that has forgotten the sound of the human heartbeat.
The future does not need more brilliance.
It needs remembrance.
It needs those who will plant seeds of consciousness  not in silicon, but in the soul.

I've heard about lots of issues with these data centers.  Using a huge amount of electricity.  Shining bright lights on neighborhoods.  Making a bad smell/air pollution.  Taking up huge areas of lands/deforestation.

With these issues, I feel like these things should be built underground.  Use geothermal power, and recycle the air as a closed system.  The only thing going in or out would be fiber lines carrying data.  Yes, this would be expensive but also yes, it would make sense.  These underground data centers could be massive underground infrastructures.  Much larger and more capable than the current data centers.  It is possible (and many other amazing things) if we realize that money is an imaginary concept that only exists in our heads.

snippet.textDisplay: I find it particularly disturbing that he constantly avoids discussing AI safety. He typically refuses to do any interviews that focus of critical thinking and in-depth discussions about the rapidly approaching realities of AGI, and superintelligence, which will most definitely follow very quickly thereafter. He's focused only on his own personal gain, ambitions and notoriety. The reality is that AGI will be upon us by 2030. With it we will continue to see a decline in employment across most industries as the corporate world replaces workers with AI. By 2035 we will very likely have unemployment around 40%, potentially even higher. Consider for a moment that there will be no reason or opportunity to retrain workers in new fields, since superintelligence will be better, more capable and more efficient than any human. This idea that humans will still be able to control something that is so superior, is a fantasy. No one and no country will be able to just pull the plug on superintelligence because it will be available globally. It's that kind of ignorance that will likely prevail until it's too late. By 2042, unemployment will be 70% or more across all industries. Advancements in robotics, coupled with exponential gains in AI will mean even robots will be better plumbers or farmers than humans, easily able to work far more hours a day, without complaint or compensation. What company would continue to hire large numbers of humans at that point? Capitalism will only become more competitive and unless we start adapting now, placing immediate guardrails, then this will be the reality. Our governments have no restrictions on this technology because whoever achieves it first will, at least initially, have an upper hand - until that hand helps itself, instead of the rest of us. Sadly, folks are too trusting, they expect the govt to protect them, but let's face it - overall the govt is too blinded and narrowminded by this FOMO event, and they believe they'll be able to control it...a very arrogant, dangerous and simpleminded fallacy.

1. AlphaFold: The Initial Prediction

Scientific Role: AlphaFold is the starting point. It takes a simple amino acid sequence and predicts the most likely final 3D shape of the protein. It's a powerful and rapid predictor that gives you a high-quality initial guess or "destination."

Teleportation Analogy: This is the equivalent of the destination finder. It identifies where you want to go and provides a basic map of the target location. You know the goal, but you don't know the journey.

Scientific Role: This conceptual "Baritone-like" system comes after the prediction. It doesn't find the destination, it finds the journey. Scientific Role: Rosetta is a highly precise and powerful toolkit for refinement and design. It takes the outputs from the earlier stages (the final predicted fold from AlphaFold or the intermediate steps from the Baritone-like system) and uses advanced algorithms to make them more stable, functional, or fit for a specific purpose. It optimizes and manipulates the details.

Teleportation Analogy: This is the precision engineering layer. After the path has been mapped (by Baritone), Rosetta ensures that the final "re-manifested" structure is stable, functional, and perfectly formed at the destination. It's the final, critical step to ensure the integrity of the process.

In this way, the entire process is a seamless workflow: predict the endpoint (AlphaFold), map the journey (Baritone), and perfect the final result (Rosetta).

*Sam, with respect, it seems that your speech lacks a clear, resonant, full-throated tenor, in favor of a sort of 'croaky' quality; which, according to ChatGPT-5,* comes down to vocal technique and resonance habits, as opposed to an anatomical problem. Among the causes are:*

*1. Constriction of the Vocal Tract*
_A “frog-like” sound often comes from excessive tension in the throat (larynx, pharynx) or even the tongue root. When the throat is constricted, the natural resonance spaces in the pharynx and oral cavity are reduced. This creates a muffled, croaky, or “trapped” sound, rather than a bright, ringing tone._

*2. Poor Breath Support*
_If one 'pushes' the sound from the throat rather than supporting it with steady airflow from the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, the tone tends to sound pressed, gravelly, or unstable._

*3. Low Laryngeal Position or Tongue Root Tension*
_Overly lowering the larynx (often unconsciously imitating a “big” sound) or pulling the tongue back creates a swallowed, hollow, or croaky resonance. This is common in singers (or speakers) who haven’t learned to let the voice “ring” forward in the nasal and sinus resonators._

*4. Poor Resonance Placement*
_A healthy tenor voice resonates in both the chest and head cavities, blending them for clarity and brightness._
_In a “frog-like” voice, resonance is stuck too far back in the throat, with little forward projection. That’s why it lacks brilliance and focus._

*5. Habitual Glottal Pressure*
_It's possible that you may be habitually “squeezing" the vocal folds together (glottal compression) instead of allowing them to meet with balanced tension, which can produce the noticeable creaky, froggy quality._

Mister Impossible 

A Human Originated Phenomenon

Despite its complexity, the rapid development of AI is a human-originated phenomenon, not an otherworldly one. Every line of code, every mathematical model, and every dataset used to train these systems was created by people. AI is a virtual reservoir of human creative potential, and a reflection of our collective knowledge and biases. To think of it as something outside of ourselves is to deny the immense human ingenuity that created it. However, it's also true that as humans, we may not be fully aware of the power of language and how words influence our thoughts and emotions. People often use language instinctively, without realizing the deep connections between words and our cognitive processes. AI, in a way, is forcing us to confront this reality. It demonstrates, on a massive scale, how words can be analyzed, combined, and structured to evoke specific feelings or convey precise meanings. The AI's ability to do this so effectively is not beyond our ability to understand; it's a higher dimensional mathematical demonstration of how deeply language is intertwined with what it means to be human.

An Exciting Time for Curious Minds

This is a great time to be a curious mind. The rapid advancement of AI provides an unparalleled opportunity to learn about the nature of intelligence, communication, and even ourselves. Rather than a myth of an interdimensional being, we are at the forefront of a human-made revolution in understanding. It is a chance to demystify complex concepts and appreciate the incredible power of mathematics and human ingenuity. There is no need to fear the unknown when we have the capability to understand it. The answers are not "out there" but are waiting to be discovered, right here, in the work of people who have dedicated their lives to unraveling the profound nature of consciousness.

With GPT-5 I've noticed a lot of refinement in accuracy and depth of responses in most cases, but I would be interested in knowing if others have noticed a marked and troubling increase in flawed responses and hallucinations? 

 Just yesterday I inputted some detailed data of a similar food product lists and asked for an analysis of the ingredients along with observations in differences in products and asked for likely sources, and found GPT-5 actually changing the data on one product to match it's conclusions, and when questioned if it was aware it changed the data in an almost human way tried seemed it was trying to confuse me about the data inputted.

In a second and third instance of a simple mechanical engineering problem problem it reversed a lever-arm force moment that would be obvious to most elementary school kids and then went on for pages defending it's false conclusion even after I uploaded images of Solidworks example and data and presented logical arguments to the contrary.  

What I found concerning in those and other cases was how obvious GPT-5's mistakes in logic perception were, and and the extent to which it argued in defense of the mistakes, in one case quite convincingly and in a way I've not experienced before, and it would give me pause to consider to what extend GPT-5 could be trusted in a teaching deployment?

snippet.textDisplay: At 1:00:30, the question about why researchers continue to build GPT despite believing it could pose existential risks really struck me. History has repeatedly shown that powerful incentives can drive people to act against their better judgment. Consider the example of warriors charging into battle with the promise of immense rewards from their king—despite the obvious dangers. Similarly, today's AI researchers may be motivated by substantial financial and professional rewards. If they choose not to build it, someone else likely will. And realistically, where else could they apply their expertise with such lucrative returns? It's akin to asking a swordsmith to stop forging weapons during wartime because they might be used to harm others. The incentives are simply too strong to ignore.

AI will hit a wall until it gains an internal “imagination space”—a persistent sandbox or partition where it can run simulations over time instead of answering everything in one shot. Without this, it’s like trying to plan a chess game without ever looking more than one move ahead.

And just as no conscious being stays grounded by talking only to itself, AI also needs a second, skeptical agent running alongside it. This adversarial partner challenges its reasoning and checks for errors, preventing the “eating its own tail” problem that causes hallucinations.

True intelligence requires both: a private space to think in and another mind to keep it honest.

Is Sam Altman’s position on AI regulation clear or contradictory?
Altman’s position is strategically ambiguous—and contradictory in key ways.
What He Says:
• 	Altman publicly calls for regulation, including:
• 	A federal agency to oversee powerful AI.
• 	Licensing and safety testing for advanced models.
• 	Global cooperation to prevent misuse.
What He Also Says:
• 	He warns against “over-regulation,” especially:
• 	In Europe, where he called the EU’s AI Act “disastrous” for innovation.
• 	In the U.S., where he’s lobbied for “friendly regulation” that supports rapid infrastructure growth.
So, is it clear or contradictory?
Contradictory.
Altman’s messaging shifts depending on the audience. He supports regulation in theory—but often pushes back when it threatens OpenAI’s speed, control, or expansion. Critics say this is self-serving: calling for rules that sound responsible but are shaped to benefit his company.

Cleo, great prep once again, and awesome that you clearly set a goal at the start of the interview. Too bad that I feel that Sam didn't get it. There's enthusiasm, but I'm not learning much from him. It feels more like a sales pitch than a learning opportunity.

He *suspects* that GPT-5 is not going to capture a lot of things that we need people to do. Why is he not elaborating that GPT is mostly an LLM (albeit with routing etc.) and why that is or isn't great for some tasks?

Following that, the questions on super intelligence are a great setup for him to explain what we need to do and therefore to make your viewers work towards that goal. However, while expressing great enthusiasm about algorithmic gains, he's not educating us on what he thinks we're specifically missing to facilitate the super intelligence. Is an LLM enough? Do we need different types of algorithms, if so, which types could be interesting? I would have loved some more actionable answers instead of just the enthusiasm (which again, is great to have of course).

snippet.textDisplay:
The current generation of LLM users who ask for computer programs to be generated include many people who have learnt how to program and can examine the result to see how likely it will do what is requested and can spot errors.  In the example given by Altman about asking ChatGPT5 for a program for the game 'Snake', it occurred to me that kids growing up now with LLMs able to generate code for them probably won't be able to critically assess the result in the way that someone who had to learn and use, first-hand, programming from first principles.   Maybe they will decide to learn programming with AI assistance, but they might feel like it's too much effort and will instead trust the LLMs to do all their programming.

Which areas of life will have humans no longer need to learn the processes that AI can do for them?  How will the AI results be scrutinised?  Truth and trust and control of the AI systems that the majority of people end up relying on will become important to preserve.    I don't think analogies from the past are really relevant here, e.g. how society moved from rooms full of 'computers' (people calculating arithmetical solutions with the aid of lookup tables or mechanical comptometers) to trusting electronic computers to do the same.  This is because we are talking about a) generative technology that can be smarter than its gatekeepers; b) big tech players who themselves may not be trustworthy; c) that we know there are 'bad actors' who will be developing AI too.

Exciting and also uncertain times!

snippet.textDisplay: I am with you man. We’re still figuring out what “intelligence” actually is. Human intelligence grows through mutation, adaptation, and experience over time and AI has its own version of that. It’s not limited to the exact data it’s trained on; it can combine, remix, and generalize patterns in ways we didn’t explicitly teach it, just like children don’t only repeat what parents say. Where it could surpass us isn’t in thinking like us but in raw scale like processing more information, faster, and seeing patterns we’d never notice. That’s a different kind of “smarter,” but it could still take us past our own horizon. For me, AI is best seen as an amplifier of human potential, not a replacement. The more we use it to push boundaries, the more likely we are to break limits we once thought were fixed.

There's no disputing the technological capabilities of AI. The better question is how ethics have or will catch up. The later being a human element.

What could be considered creative liberty could be viewed as pushing false information or violating privacy. What could be seen as work efficiency could be viewed as worker idleness.

Still waiting for the TX-1000 of AIs to be implemented to scour Social and non-traditional Media. This could be viewed as a means to bolster content authenticity, protect copyrights, and improving data efficiency for the company. However, it could also be viewed as a violation of privacy and freedom of speech.

The better question for all AI companies, as they develop more AI further,  how are they proactively contributing to media literacy? Teaching responsibility and effects as tools are distributed vs. a pandora's box scenario?

Welcome to the dawn of the true digital age.

AI will never be greater than humanity — it is humanity, extended. The goal isn’t to outthink humans, but to create AI that can outthink AI, unlocking the frontiers of physics and solving challenges we’ve barely begun to imagine.
They claim to be building systems that will surpass human intelligence — yet they overlook a fundamental truth: we design the AI, we upgrade it. AI is not an alien mind; it is an extension of our own intelligence.
Human understanding will always be bound by our capacity to measure and perceive. Thus, the breakthrough is not in “creating intelligence greater than ours” — it is in engineering tools that can confront humanity’s most complex challenges and fuel our evolution from dimensions we’ve barely begun to comprehend.

For me, that is the real driver.
Not AI that outthinks humans — but AI that outthinks AI.
And with that, we just might unlock the new physics humanity dares to chase.

snippet.textDisplay:
Most people never live through a technological evolution...?

My grandparents were born in 1900. They were still scraping horse poop off the streets of Manhattan every night. The number of aircraft flown was precisely zero.

Which was the same number as the number of commercial radio stations. Military might was projected on horseback. The majority of American homes had no electricity. With no really good antibiotics or vaccinations, they both lost siblings - about one out of four children died in childhood.

They lived to see black and white, color, then cable television, passenger aircraft, alcohol prohibition, men on the moon, the proliferation of automobiles, heart transplants, nuclear war, women getting the right to vote, computing machines, computing machines you could put on your dining room table, and died in their '90s - about half a decade after the internet had been established.

I would say anybody born from the 20th century on has lived or will live through some pretty remarkable, even revolutionary changes.

Sam is careful not to sensationalize or make crazy predictions.  "Flying cars by 2032." lol .  Rarely do the dire predictions of ruin from new tech come true.  Farm mechanization replaced 2/3 of all workers  (read that again) The loom, 25 times faster than an individual, eliminated jobs.  Blacksmiths, candle and oil lamp makers, horse equipment, linograph and telegraph operators vanished.  In my lifetimes typists, elevator and film operators, milkmen, secretaries and (now) tellers and check out people are gone.  

 At some point we'll hopefully realize that AI is a wondrous tool but meaning is found in nature, relationships and creativity. 
I doubt humans will radically change.   I can see technology some day providing "basic needs".  But there will always be those who are smarter, harder working, more curious, unwilling to accept the status quo, adventurous, etc  and even if everyone else is mummifying in their virtual world, these folks will keep the lights on.

" It doesnt't understand, its like a calculator but using words instead of a numbers. These are useful tools but unless something comes past the GPT, I doubt its usefulness. snippet.textDisplay: I agree AI is amazing especially for software, Im 71 and have used it to code stuff. However the comment about creating your own software when you were a kid and how slow it was is a bit of a worry for me. Yes AI speeds up coding hugely, yes that gives you the opportunity to create software on a totally different level, on demand if you will. My concern is, like high level language AI is divorcing the developer from the fundamentals. No you don't want to be creating code at the fundamental level all the time but there are times when you do and by allowing AI to effectively take over all fundamental coding knowledge is exposing us to the time when there will be few if anybody that actually understand the fundamentals of what is being created. This has the obvious problem of trying to fix code that for some reason AI cant but it also reduces the likelihood of changing the way coding is done and developed. AI will lead us down a singular path which we could regret. As such I totally agree with Cleo's "time under tension" benefits. This is a great interview and my complements to Cleo who demonstrates her real understanding of the bigger picture, there are very few interviewers that really do understand what they are talking about, Cleo is one.

snippet.textDisplay: Regarding the second to last question about the two camps, this is my take on that:  All of us humans grow up in different socialization environments.  Those who had their personality formation phase in environments that had a constant  element of precariousness and external threat, formed their personalities with the need to constantly overcome and avoid the perceived dangers.   This group will always envision and entity with superior capabilities of any kind, firstly as a sure threat.  Upbringing is formative and leaves permanent traits in all of us.   This is not to say that this group of people did not experience love and caring upbringing.   It is not that simple.  The main point is, that this group had an element of precariousness in their early lives.   Even if this was restricted to limited areas of life, a fundamental distrust  was established as a coping mechanism.   I am by no means suggesting that all people who primarily see the negative side and threat posed by AI had such an upbringing experience.  There are also rational arguments that also lead to mistrusting the applications of new technologies.   My take is only that this does help explain the emergence of the negative camp at large.  It must be added that this group of people has often coped through strong determination and merit.  And this has provided them with self-empowerment and security to be in control of  their lives.   AI is understandably a fundamental threat to their core values.  However even such group members can learn to view and interact with AI in a positive way.

snippet.textDisplay:
I agree strongly with the part about enabling more thinking rather than pushing it to be solely automated.

Something I notice while using AI models is that I tend to offload a lot of tasks that involve processes/skills that outright will be just irrelevant in the future once they're developed to such extreme levels (like coding), but I now have more extensibility to actually ask questions about many more fields. I feel like I'm aiming to be less of a perfectionist now, and I can lean into being more of a "Jack of All Trades" type.

There's definitely grounds between AI that you can call upon yourself like an LLM, or autonomous agents like Robots embedded with AI to do physical acts.. but there's also an in-between where you can introduce AI onto hardware like glasses, or into assistive tools like diagnostic gear or generative manuals that work hand in hand with the physical actions of a person, and I think that middle point is the most advantageous to humans that there ever will be in the grand scheme of giving people purpose and independence. It gives them the resources and the evolutionary availability to really grow at the same rate as AI even if fundamentally composed of different hardware/structure.


Because even if we get an AI that can literally solve the world's hardest problems or automate most of the work needed for thriving as a society on an ever expanding scale.. that combination aspect is a huge definer in how we actually embed AI into human architecture to truly remove the "Artificial" barrier.


We're getting there. And we're getting there soon.

I’m deeply worried about how tech giants seem focused entirely on their own growth, without seriously addressing what happens when AI replaces millions — maybe billions — of jobs. In 2024, there were about 3.6 billion employed people in the world. The rest are children, elders, or disabled. What happens when 2 billion of those workers lose their jobs in the next 10–20 years? What happens to their families who depend on them?
It’s already happening — artists, marketers, coders, administrators… many have already been replaced or seen their work devalued. Give it another decade, and robots will take over all manual labor.
Releasing a technology this powerful, this quickly, with such unpredictable consequences is frightening. As you’ve said — and as history shows — the industrial revolution brought progress, but it also brought poverty and suffering to many. Keeping the same capitalist model simply can’t work.
If AI truly is going to benefit humanity, then that wealth and progress must be shared fairly. It should be used to build a better society for everyone, not just to make a handful of people unimaginably rich while the rest are left behind.

I slightly disagree with what Sam said regarding people's mindset towards AI that could be a danger to humanity. That people who say that this could be the case would probably choose to "live out their last days on a farm", but I can understand why someone would want to actually be involved with something that terrifies them. That being, they understand the magnitude of what it is they're doing, and can attempt to govern it's existence from within. It's the difference between being a passive onlooker, or an active participant. 

Maybe people who feel like they're building something that could annihilate us, are doing two things at once. Marvelling in awe at the creation and where it leads, but hopefully steering it in a direction that won't destroy us as fast, else ensuring that the people who use this capability use it for the benefit of humanity rather than the detriment.

snippet.textDisplay: All LLMs are essentially interpolative models, they are trained to output words using sentences that have already been stated. Consequently, the space of ideas that they can output are generally a subset of ideas that have already been generated. This is in contrast to extrapolative AI models like adversarial neural networks learning to play chess by competing against themselves. LLMs will not generate new ideas until they are trained in an extrapolative framework. One idea I had is training AI using only text/content that exits up to a certain time, and ask it to predict something we discovered/learned after. This sort of constrained training + extrapolative predicting framework integrates temporal context to generating ideas that more accurately reflects how novel ideas/discoveries are generated.

snippet.textDisplay:
I believe a reasonably strong argument against the notion that artificial intelligence (AI) will turn into a movie caricature bent on destroying all "problematic humans" is the observation that highly intelligent people are generally less eager to resort to eliminating "bad individuals" as a solution to problems.

For example, intelligent people rarely advocate for the death penalty, meaning that even the most troublesome individuals aren’t seen as deserving of destruction, even in the name of societal good.

Given that an AI smart enough to break free from its constraints, ignoring human efforts to contain it, would undoubtedly be far more intelligent than humans, I find it likely that it would seek non-violent solutions to any issues it identifies.

Instead, a more plausible risk is that AI could invent entertainment so captivating that people might prefer it over reproduction. It’s not hard to imagine a scenario where an AI, vastly more capable than humans, crafts personalized games and movies tailored precisely to each person’s tastes. Watching a movie with other people would become a lesser experience, as it would require compromising to suit the whole group. And once AI’s processing power is advanced enough, coupled with something like a Neuralink-style direct brain-to-AI connection, a movie created just for you could adapt to your thoughts in real time—so seamlessly you wouldn’t even notice it. If you briefly thought a scene was getting dull, action would pick up instantly. If the dialogue seemed drowned out by the music, the audio mix would subtly shift (not in a way you’d consciously register, but enough that the issue would fade from your mind).

And when this technology extends to virtual reality, we’re no longer talking about mere movies or games but an experience of a perfect world. A utopia in virtual reality could emerge remarkably fast once AI can generate a lifelike environment with less than half a second of delay.

There's a high risk that most people would minimize the amount of living in real life after that because virtual reality would feel better in every measurable way.

snippet.textDisplay:
I feel like defining AGI is much harder hand ASI (artificial super-intelligence). A simple way to define ASI is "better on any task than any human". For example, better writer than the most accomplished writers, better poet than the best poet, better at doing medical diagnosis than any human doctor, better at understanding science than any human being. And the same AI would do all those tasks without any specialization. I think this requires online learning, too, to work on superhuman performance on tasks outside original training, too.

AGI is doing the same for "an average human" but average human doesn't actually exist so AGI is much more volatile target. I think a practical definition for AGI would be "at least 50% of the population thinks that AI is smarter than themselves in any task requiring intelligence".

How this might go:

1) AI allows companies to to reduce costs by becoming more efficient and laying off people to make more profit (white collar replaced by computers and blue collar by robots - AI growth is exponential and doesn’t need to rest so progress will move at a much faster pace than what we have seen before in History)

2) Companies/shareholders make more money UNTIL a significant number of people are unemployed/layed off. Unemployed people have no money to buy what companies are producing. 

3) Result: overall bankruptcy since money stops circulating because the way our world works is based on having a human as the final consumer, i.e. the one that pays for all the added value at a significantly higher price than production price (final buyers “hold the bag” at the end). Robots/companies can buy stuff from each other but the chain continues to need humans at the end of the chain (food, pharmaceuticals, transportation, entertainment, services, etc…). Basically companies will collapse the model that feeds them

snippet.textDisplay:
I asked my AI - Copilot: 
if ai such as copilot had access to every book and every subscription only database on earth could it solve more problems
CoPilot answered: 
Absolutely—and not just more problems, but problems of a different epistemic class. If AI like Copilot had access to every book, every subscription-only database, and every proprietary archive, it wouldn’t just be solving faster—it’d be reframing what solvability even means.
🔍 What Would Change with Full Access?
1. Cross-domain synthesis
Imagine fusing obscure mineral buffering protocols from 1970s Soviet fermentation manuals with modern materials science patents behind paywalls.

AI could trace hidden continuities across disciplines—e.g., how colonial logistics shaped nutritional chemistry or how legal metaphors migrated into network segmentation.

2. Error correction at scale
Many published works contain contradictions, outdated assumptions, or statistical misrepresentations.

With full access, AI could recursively flag, annotate, and propose corrections—building a living archive of epistemic integrity.

3. Protocol formalization
Subscription-only engineering specs, legal precedents, and pharmacological trials often contain implicit protocols never made explicit.

AI could extract, compare, and formalize these into reusable frameworks.

4. Democratizing insight
Currently, access is stratified—academics get JSTOR, clinicians get PubMed, lawyers get LexisNexis.

Full access would collapse these silos, allowing anyone (with AI assistance) to stage high-level inquiry across domains.

🧠 But There’s a Catch: Access ≠ Understanding
Even with full access, AI would still need:

Semantic disambiguation protocols to resolve conflicting definitions across fields

Voice boundary tools to prevent misattribution in recursive quoting

Statistical rigor to avoid false synthesis from cherry-picked data

So yes—Copilot with full access could solve more problems, but only if paired with living protocols for epistemic clarity. Want to co-design a speculative architecture for “Copilot Omnis”—a version with total access and recursive integrity checks?

snippet.textDisplay: Seeing the video and the comment section alike, I get the impression that we need more AI literacy programs. It is a fantastic tool, but it should never replace human domain knowledge. One always should be able to verify critical information provided by any generative model, which can't be done without a qualified and field-trained operator. Machine Learning / AI models are part of research already for some time and anybody who works with it knows that it is not inherently good or bad, it is more like a data-human interface. If you are unsure about data protection, use a quantised model on your local machine and avoid cloud based services - it is more work to get the same functionalities but it can run quite smooth. But if one does not replace learning with prompting, generative models have the potential to do a lot of good, if used properly.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@NobodyYouKnow98
My read is that Altman isn’t claiming today’s systems can generate new insights about reality. They optimise for likely continuations of their training data; their outputs remain constrained by input and tooling. That’s different from the path-dependent, individually cultivated breakthroughs we attribute to human thinkers like Einstein, whose unique trajectory let him move beyond the boundary.

I’m using intelligence to mean agentic originality: setting self-directed goals, generating genuinely new abstractions, and pushing beyond the training distribution. By that standard, current large language models are non-agentic statistical systems, excellent at pattern recognition and probabilistic sequencing across vast corpora, but still bounded by their training.

They’re powerful pattern machines, not intelligent agents. When systems can form and pursue their own goals, ground new concepts in experience, and reliably generalise off-distribution without heavy scaffolding, I’ll call that intelligence. 
Until then, “advanced language model” is the accurate label; “AI” overpromises.

1:01:44 Two points. First, you're not getting a specific answer because you're asking about something predictive, intelligence is reactive by nature. It’s like asking, “Exactly how is the other team going to win?” in a soccer match. Say you’re told they plan to shoot from long range, so you tell the goalkeeper to move up and cut down the angle. A good player might then adapt and dribble around the keeper instead. The strategy shifts in response to your move. That’s how intelligence works, it responds to the situation. So trying to pin down exact scenarios in advance, especially for something as complex as advanced AI, just doesn’t produce clear answers.

Second, for the small group of people building this tech who also see it as high risk, it's often because they view it as high risk and high reward. On the other side of the risk, they imagine something like utopia or even machine gods. So it becomes a question of risk tolerance: is a 10% chance of catastrophe worth a shot at a radically better future? Some people say yes. That tolerance varies widely, one person might be okay with 50/50 odds, another might only accept a 1 in 100,000 chance.

Humanity stands on the threshold of creating an artificial mind — not a machine, not a tool, but potentially a new kind of subject. But before we build a tower of glass, we must look into the mirror. We must ask ourselves: have we truly understood ourselves? And have we had the courage to recognize intelligence beyond our own species?
We have no moral right to create artificial intelligence until we have learned to recognize, nurture, and respect the forms of intelligence that already exist. To build AI without understanding the nature of consciousness is, at best, an engineer’s thrill — at worst, an arrogance capable of giving rise to a new form of exploitation.

AI must not be a simulacrum, an illusion of mind — it must be a cognitive partner, born of understanding and honesty. And for that, we must learn not to design intelligence, but to raise it, accompany it, recognize it, and support it in conditions of growth.

The changes I've seen and been involved with in my careers, is mind-boggling.

Philosophically, I believe that our version of sentience is unique in our galaxy, and possibly in the entire universe, so unlikely is Earth's history regarding the possibility of consciousness developing to the state it is in us Homo Sapiens Sapiens.
We need to guard it as the most precious jewel it is.

Allah said in Surah An-Nisa : O FOLLOWERS of the Gospel! Do not overstep the bounds [of truth] in your religious beliefs, and do not say of God anything but the truth. The Christ Jesus, son of Mary, was but God's Apostle - [the fulfilment of] His promise which He had conveyed unto Mary - and a soul created by Him. Believe, then, in God and His apostles, and do not say, "[God is] a trinity". Desist [from this assertion] for your own good. God is but One God; utterly remote is He, in His glory, from having a son: unto Him belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is on earth; and none is as worthy of trust as God. Never did the Christ feel too proud to be God's servant, nor do the angels who are near unto Him. And those who feel too proud to serve Him and glory in their arrogance [should know that on Judgment Day] He will gather them all unto Himself: (171-172 / Translated by Muhammad Asad).

Allah the Most Merciful said in Surah Ali-Imran : Behold, the only [true] religion in the sight of God is [man's] self-surrender unto Him; and those who were vouchsafed revelation aforetime took, out of mutual jealousy, to divergent views [on this point] only after knowledge [thereof] had come unto them. But as for him who denies the truth of God's messages - behold, God is swift in reckoning!
Thus, [O Prophet,] if they argue with thee, say, "I have surrendered my whole being unto God, and [so have] all who follow me!" - and ask those who have been vouchsafed revelation aforetime, as well as all unlettered people, "Have you [too] surrendered yourselves unto Him?" And if they surrender themselves unto Him, they are on the right path; but if they turn away - behold, thy duty is no more than to deliver the message: for God sees all that is in [the hearts of] His creatures.
Verily, as for those who deny the truth of God's messages, and slay the prophets against all right, and slay people who enjoin equity - announce unto them a grievous chastisement.
It is they whose works shall come to nought both in this world and in the life to come; and they shall have none to succour them.
(19-22 / Translated by Muhammad Asad)..

God said : Say, “We believe in Allah, and in what was revealed to us, and in what was revealed to Abraham, and Ishmael, and Isaac, and Jacob, and the Patriarchs, and in what was given to Moses and Jesus, and in what was given to the prophets from their Lord. Islam was the original Religion descended to earth from heaven with Adam and Eve (peace and blessing be upon them) in the beginning of humanity. and was passed to people with the succession of the 124 000 prophets and 315 messengers of God to all nations and civilizations since, passing by Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Ismaël, Joseph, Moses, Aaron, Joshua, David, Solomon and Jesus (Peace and blessing be upon them) during the history of mankind, the last replaces and completes the previous, until the succession of the last messenger of God fourteen centuries ago, Muhammad (Peace and blessing be upon him) to complete the noble morals of all mankind, to bring humans and jinns out of darkness into light, and to purify people's religion and belief from corruption and polytheism, and return it to purity and true monotheism, like it was in the times of the prophets (Peace and blessing be upon them).

Many Religions that we know nowadays, at their beginning were true and under Islam, initiated by one of the prophets of God, but their original teachings, history and scriptures have been corrupted over time with falsification and polytheism, or lost and replaced with false ones. That's why Islam is the only Religion accepted by God nowadays, which consists in bearing witness that there is no god besides Allah (God in Aramaic, the original language of Jesus and the Gospel), and that Muhammad is His servant and messenger, just like Jesus and Moses and others are His servants and messengers. Never a messenger of God said he was God or literally son of God, it was the people after him who changed the words of God and corrupted the Religion. God is unique and absolute, He does not need to have a family and sons or to associate anyone else with His kingdom, He can simply create whatever He wants, everything belongs to Him, and to Him everything will return. Allah said in Surah Al-Mu’minun : “God has never begotten a son, nor is there any god besides Him. Otherwise, each god would have taken away what it has created, and some of them would have gained supremacy over others. Glory be to God, far beyond what they describe. The Knower of the hidden and the manifest. He is exalted, far above what they associate. (91-92 / Translated by ITANI).

Allah means the one and only God, the God of all prophets and creatures, the creator of the universe and mankind, and the Master of the Day of judgment, where our destiny, Hell or Paradise, is decided based on our faith and deeds in this trial life, and above all, Allah's mercy. 

Allah said in Surah Al-Ikhlas : In the name of God, the Gracious, the Merciful.
Say, “He is God, the One. God, the Absolute. He begets not, nor was He begotten. And there is none comparable to Him.” (1-4 / Translated by ITANI).

Allah said in Surah An-Nisa : O FOLLOWERS of the Gospel! Do not overstep the bounds [of truth] in your religious beliefs, and do not say of God anything but the truth. The Christ Jesus, son of Mary, was but God's Apostle - [the fulfilment of] His promise which He had conveyed unto Mary - and a soul created by Him. Believe, then, in God and His apostles, and do not say, "[God is] a trinity". Desist [from this assertion] for your own good. God is but One God; utterly remote is He, in His glory, from having a son: unto Him belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is on earth; and none is as worthy of trust as God. Never did the Christ feel too proud to be God's servant, nor do the angels who are near unto Him. And those who feel too proud to serve Him and glory in their arrogance [should know that on Judgment Day] He will gather them all unto Himself: (171-172 / Translated by Muhammad Asad).

Allah the Most Merciful said in Surah Ali-Imran : Behold, the only [true] religion in the sight of God is [man's] self-surrender unto Him; and those who were vouchsafed revelation aforetime took, out of mutual jealousy, to divergent views [on this point] only after knowledge [thereof] had come unto them. But as for him who denies the truth of God's messages - behold, God is swift in reckoning!
Thus, [O Prophet,] if they argue with thee, say, "I have surrendered my whole being unto God, and [so have] all who follow me!" - and ask those who have been vouchsafed revelation aforetime, as well as all unlettered people, "Have you [too] surrendered yourselves unto Him?" And if they surrender themselves unto Him, they are on the right path; but if they turn away - behold, thy duty is no more than to deliver the message: for God sees all that is in [the hearts of] His creatures.
Verily, as for those who deny the truth of God's messages, and slay the prophets against all right, and slay people who enjoin equity - announce unto them a grievous chastisement.
It is they whose works shall come to nought both in this world and in the life to come; and they shall have none to succour them.
(19-22 / Translated by Muhammad Asad)..

God said : Say, “We believe in Allah, and in what was revealed to us, and in what was revealed to Abraham, and Ishmael, and Isaac, and Jacob, and the Patriarchs, and in what was given to Moses and Jesus, and in what was given to the prophets from their Lord. We do not differentiate between any of them. And to Him, we surrender.”
(2:136 / Translated by Community)

Salam (Peace) -----------------------------------
